ca.holomorphic.title: Holomorphic functions
ca.holomorphic.define: Complex differentiability throughout an open set imposes strong local rigidity.
ca.holomorphic.statement: A function on an open set $U\subset\mathbb C$ is holomorphic if the complex derivative exists at every point of $U$. This is stronger than real differentiability.
ca.holomorphic.hypotheses: The derivative limit must be independent of the direction of approach.
ca.holomorphic.example: $z^2$ is holomorphic; $\bar z$ is not holomorphic on any nonempty open set.
ca.holomorphic.caution: Complex differentiability at one isolated point does not imply local holomorphy.
ca.holomorphic.prerequisites:
**From other subjects**

- [Metric limits and completeness](./notes/ra.metric.md) — Real analysis
ca.holomorphic.references:
CA: analytic functions.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.cr.title: Cauchy–Riemann equations
ca.cr.define: The real differential of a holomorphic function is complex linear.
ca.cr.statement: For $f=u+iv$ with real $C^1$ components, holomorphy is equivalent to $u_x=v_y$ and $u_y=-v_x$. Equivalently, $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$.
ca.cr.hypotheses: The sufficient condition here assumes continuous first partial derivatives on an open set.
ca.cr.caution: Pointwise equations without regularity are not the stated sufficient criterion.
ca.cr.proof_idea: Identify the real differential with multiplication by a complex number.
ca.cr.references:
CA: analytic functions.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.series.title: Power series and analyticity
ca.series.define: A complex power series converges locally uniformly inside its radius of convergence and may be differentiated termwise there. Holomorphic functions locally equal their Taylor series.
ca.series.statement: A complex power series converges locally uniformly inside its radius of convergence and may be differentiated termwise there. Holomorphic functions locally equal their Taylor series.
ca.series.hypotheses: Taylor expansion is inside a disk contained in the domain of holomorphy.
ca.series.caution: Real smoothness does not imply analyticity; boundary convergence needs a separate argument.
ca.series.proof_idea: Use uniform convergence on smaller disks and Cauchy estimates for the Taylor remainder.
ca.series.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Cauchy integral formula](./notes/ca.cauchy-formula.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Uniform convergence](./notes/ra.uniform.md) — Real analysis
ca.series.references:

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.contours.title: Contour integrals and winding number
ca.contours.define: Winding number measures the signed turns of a closed contour around a point.
ca.contours.statement: For a piecewise $C^1$ closed curve $\gamma$ and $a$ off its image, $\operatorname{Ind}(\gamma,a)=(2\pi i)^{-1}\int_\gamma dz/(z-a)$ is an integer.
ca.contours.hypotheses: Orientation and the parametrized curve, including repeated traversal, matter.
ca.contours.example: A positively oriented circle winds once around its center and zero times around an exterior point.
ca.contours.caution: Being geometrically enclosed is inadequate for self-intersecting or multiply traversed curves.
ca.contours.references:
CA: line integrals; general Cauchy theorem.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.cauchy.title: Cauchy–Goursat theorem
ca.cauchy.define: Holomorphic functions have zero closed-contour integrals on simply connected domains.
ca.cauchy.statement: If $f$ is holomorphic on a simply connected domain $U$, then $\int_\gamma f(z)\,dz=0$ for every closed piecewise $C^1$ curve in $U$.
ca.cauchy.hypotheses: The entire curve lies in the domain. Holomorphy does not require an a priori continuous derivative.
ca.cauchy.example: The integral of $1/z$ around the unit circle is nonzero because the punctured plane is not simply connected.
ca.cauchy.caution: The general homological version requires a null-homologous cycle in the domain.
ca.cauchy.proof_idea: Prove the triangle theorem by subdivision, then construct primitives locally and use simple connectivity.
ca.cauchy.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Contour integrals and winding number](./notes/ca.contours.md)
ca.cauchy.references:
CA: Cauchy–Goursat; general Cauchy theorem.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.cauchy-formula.title: Cauchy integral formula
ca.cauchy-formula.define: Boundary values recover all interior derivatives of a holomorphic function.
ca.cauchy-formula.statement: If $f$ is holomorphic near a closed disk and $z$ is interior, then $f^{(n)}(z)=\frac{n!}{2\pi i}\int_{\partial D}\frac{f(\zeta)}{(\zeta-z)^{n+1}}\,d\zeta$.
ca.cauchy-formula.hypotheses: The circle is positively oriented; $n$ is a nonnegative integer.
ca.cauchy-formula.example: On a radius-$R$ circle about $z$, $|f^{(n)}(z)|\le n!\max_{\partial D}|f|/R^n$.
ca.cauchy-formula.caution: The evaluation point must stay off the integration curve.
ca.cauchy-formula.proof_idea: Apply Cauchy's theorem after removing a small disk around the evaluation point, then differentiate under the integral.
ca.cauchy-formula.references:
CA: special Cauchy formula and applications.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.identity.title: Identity theorem
ca.identity.define: Two holomorphic functions on a connected domain coincide if their agreement set has an accumulation point in that domain.
ca.identity.statement: Two holomorphic functions on a connected domain coincide if their agreement set has an accumulation point in that domain.
ca.identity.hypotheses: The accumulation point is interior, and the domain is connected.
ca.identity.example: A holomorphic function vanishing on a real interval inside its domain is identically zero.
ca.identity.caution: Zeros may accumulate at a boundary point without forcing global vanishing.
ca.identity.proof_idea: The first nonzero Taylor coefficient makes a zero isolated; propagate equality across the connected domain.
ca.identity.references:
CA: local properties of analytic functions.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.liouville.title: Liouville and the fundamental theorem of algebra
ca.liouville.define: Every bounded entire function is constant. Consequently every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.
ca.liouville.statement: Every bounded entire function is constant. Consequently every nonconstant complex polynomial has a complex root.
ca.liouville.hypotheses: Boundedness is global on the entire complex plane.
ca.liouville.example: If a polynomial had no zero, its reciprocal would be entire and bounded.
ca.liouville.caution: A bounded holomorphic function on a proper domain need not be constant.
ca.liouville.proof_idea: Let the radius in the first-derivative Cauchy estimate tend to infinity.
ca.liouville.references:
CA: Cauchy estimates.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.maximum.title: Maximum modulus principle
ca.maximum.define: A nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected domain cannot have a local interior maximum of its modulus.
ca.maximum.statement: A nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected domain cannot have a local interior maximum of its modulus.
ca.maximum.hypotheses: The maximized quantity is the modulus, not an ordering of complex values.
ca.maximum.example: For a function continuous on a closed disk and holomorphic inside, its maximum modulus is attained on the boundary.
ca.maximum.caution: The boundary conclusion requires compactness and continuous extension to the boundary.
ca.maximum.proof_idea: Use the mean-value identity and its equality case, or the local power-series expansion.
ca.maximum.references:
CA: local mapping; maximum modulus.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.singularities.title: Laurent series and isolated singularities
ca.singularities.define: An isolated singularity is removable, a pole, or essential according to whether the Laurent principal part is zero, finite nonzero, or infinite.
ca.singularities.statement: An isolated singularity is removable, a pole, or essential according to whether the Laurent principal part is zero, finite nonzero, or infinite.
ca.singularities.hypotheses: The function is holomorphic on a punctured disk.
ca.singularities.example: $\sin z/z$, $1/z^2$, and $e^{1/z}$ illustrate the three cases at zero.
ca.singularities.caution: A branch point such as zero for a logarithm is not an isolated singularity of a single-valued holomorphic function on a punctured disk.
ca.singularities.references:
CA: isolated singularities; Laurent series.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.residues.title: Residue theorem
ca.residues.define: Contour integrals of meromorphic functions reduce to weighted residues at poles.
ca.residues.statement: For a meromorphic function with finitely many poles relevant to a null-homologous contour, $\int_\gamma f\,dz=2\pi i\sum_a\operatorname{Ind}(\gamma,a)\operatorname{Res}_a f$.
ca.residues.hypotheses: The contour avoids poles and is null-homologous in the original domain before removing them.
ca.residues.example: The residue of $g(z)/(z-a)$ is $g(a)$ when $g$ is holomorphic near $a$.
ca.residues.caution: Higher-order poles require the Laurent coefficient, not simply the numerator value.
ca.residues.proof_idea: Subtract principal parts and apply Cauchy's theorem to the remaining holomorphic function.
ca.residues.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Laurent series and isolated singularities](./notes/ca.singularities.md)
- [Contour integrals and winding number](./notes/ca.contours.md)
ca.residues.references:
CA: residue theorem.

ca.argument.title: Argument principle
ca.argument.define: The winding of function values counts interior zeros minus poles.
ca.argument.statement: For a positively oriented Jordan boundary, $(2\pi i)^{-1}\int f'/f$ equals the number of zeros minus poles inside, counted with multiplicity.
ca.argument.hypotheses: The Jordan boundary is piecewise C1. The function is meromorphic near the enclosed closed region and has no zero or pole on the boundary.
ca.argument.example: A zero of order $m$ contributes residue $m$ to $f'/f$.
ca.argument.caution: Zeros on the contour invalidate the formula without an additional limiting prescription.
ca.argument.proof_idea: Compute the local residues of the logarithmic derivative.
ca.argument.references:
CA: argument principle.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.rouche.title: Rouché's theorem
ca.rouche.define: A strict boundary perturbation bound preserves the number of interior zeros.
ca.rouche.statement: If $f,g$ are holomorphic near a closed Jordan region and $|g|<|f|$ on its boundary, then $f$ and $f+g$ have the same number of interior zeros.
ca.rouche.hypotheses: Zeros are counted with multiplicity; the strict boundary inequality is the stated version.
ca.rouche.example: On $|z|=2$, $z^5$ dominates $z+1$, so $z^5+z+1$ has five zeros inside.
ca.rouche.caution: The theorem counts zeros but does not locate individual roots.
ca.rouche.proof_idea: The boundary functions $f+tg$ avoid zero, so their winding number is constant for $0\le t\le1$.
ca.rouche.references:
CA: Rouché theorem.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.schwarz.title: Schwarz lemma
ca.schwarz.define: A disk self-map fixing zero contracts radial size, with rigid equality cases.
ca.schwarz.statement: For holomorphic $f:\mathbb D\to\mathbb D$ with $f(0)=0$, $|f(z)|\le|z|$ and $|f'(0)|\le1$. Equality at a nonzero point, or in the derivative bound, forces a rotation.
ca.schwarz.hypotheses: The normalization at zero is essential to this form.
ca.schwarz.caution: For general disk maps use automorphisms and Schwarz–Pick, not the unnormalized inequality.
ca.schwarz.proof_idea: Apply the maximum principle to the removable extension of $f(z)/z$.
ca.schwarz.references:
CA: Schwarz lemma.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.normal.title: Montel's theorem
ca.normal.define: A locally uniformly bounded family of holomorphic functions on a plane domain has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets from every sequence in the family.
ca.normal.statement: A locally uniformly bounded family of holomorphic functions on a plane domain has a subsequence converging uniformly on compact subsets from every sequence in the family.
ca.normal.hypotheses: The locally bounded version yields a finite holomorphic limit; the compact-open topology is intended.
ca.normal.example: Holomorphic disk maps with values in $\mathbb D$ form a normal family.
ca.normal.caution: Pointwise boundedness is not the hypothesis, and meromorphic normality uses the spherical metric.
ca.normal.proof_idea: Cauchy estimates give equicontinuity on compact subsets; apply compactness and a diagonal exhaustion.
ca.normal.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Cauchy integral formula](./notes/ca.cauchy-formula.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Arzelà–Ascoli theorem](./notes/ra.ascoli.md) — Real analysis
ca.normal.references:
CA: normal families.

ca.riemann-mapping.title: Riemann mapping theorem
ca.riemann-mapping.define: Proper simply connected plane domains are conformally equivalent to the disk.
ca.riemann-mapping.statement: Every nonempty simply connected proper plane domain is biholomorphic to $\mathbb D$. Specifying an interior image of zero and a positive real derivative fixes the normalized inverse map uniquely.
ca.riemann-mapping.hypotheses: The domain is open, connected, simply connected, and different from the whole plane.
ca.riemann-mapping.example: The upper half-plane is mapped to the disk by a Möbius transformation.
ca.riemann-mapping.caution: The theorem does not by itself assert continuous extension to an arbitrary boundary.
ca.riemann-mapping.proof_idea: Optimize a normalized univalent family using normality; a missing image point would permit an improving map.
ca.riemann-mapping.references:
CA: Riemann mapping theorem.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.continuation.title: Analytic continuation and monodromy
ca.continuation.define: Local holomorphic germs continue uniquely along a fixed chain where overlaps agree. If a germ can be continued along every path in a simply connected domain, monodromy makes the continuation single-valued.
ca.continuation.statement: Local holomorphic germs continue uniquely along a fixed chain where overlaps agree. If a germ can be continued along every path in a simply connected domain, monodromy makes the continuation single-valued.
ca.continuation.hypotheses: Continuation along all paths is an extra existence assumption, not a consequence of simple connectivity alone.
ca.continuation.example: Continuing a logarithm around zero changes its value by an integer multiple of $2\pi i$.
ca.continuation.caution: Uniqueness on overlaps does not eliminate monodromy in a multiply connected domain.
ca.continuation.proof_idea: Use the identity theorem and deform path chains through a homotopy.
ca.continuation.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Identity theorem](./notes/ca.identity.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Homotopies and homotopy equivalence](./notes/tp.homotopy.md) — Topology
ca.continuation.references:
CA: analytic continuation; CM: Riemann surfaces.

ca.harmonic.title: Harmonic functions and conjugates
ca.harmonic.define: Harmonic functions on simply connected plane domains admit global conjugates.
ca.harmonic.statement: Real and imaginary parts of a holomorphic function are harmonic. A real $C^2$ harmonic function on a simply connected plane domain is the real part of a holomorphic function.
ca.harmonic.hypotheses: The global conjugate conclusion requires the stated topological condition.
ca.harmonic.example: $\log|z|$ is harmonic off zero but has no global single-valued harmonic conjugate on $\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}$.
ca.harmonic.caution: Harmonicity is a real second-order condition; holomorphy is a complex first-order condition.
ca.harmonic.proof_idea: The Cauchy–Riemann equations define a closed differential form whose periods vanish on a simply connected domain.
ca.harmonic.references:
CA: harmonic functions.

- **CA** — Sigurdur Helgason; notes by Hongxi Wang. [MIT 18.112: Functions of a Complex Variable](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-112-functions-of-a-complex-variable-fall-2008/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2008 lecture notes.

ca.riemann-surfaces.title: Riemann surfaces
ca.riemann-surfaces.define: A Riemann surface is a connected, Hausdorff, second-countable complex manifold of complex dimension one, with holomorphic coordinate transitions.
ca.riemann-surfaces.statement: A Riemann surface is a connected, Hausdorff, second-countable complex manifold of complex dimension one, with holomorphic coordinate transitions.
ca.riemann-surfaces.hypotheses: The topology and complex atlas are part of the structure.
ca.riemann-surfaces.example: The Riemann sphere and complex tori $\mathbb C/\Lambda$ are compact examples.
ca.riemann-surfaces.caution: A topological surface may carry many inequivalent conformal structures; compact does not mean biholomorphic to the sphere.
ca.riemann-surfaces.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Analytic continuation and monodromy](./notes/ca.continuation.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Topological manifolds](./notes/tp.manifolds.md) — Topology

ca.mittag-leffler.title: Mittag–Leffler theorem
ca.mittag-leffler.define: On a plane domain, arbitrary prescribed finite principal parts at a discrete set of points are realized by a meromorphic function with no other poles.
ca.mittag-leffler.statement: On a plane domain, arbitrary prescribed finite principal parts at a discrete set of points are realized by a meromorphic function with no other poles.
ca.mittag-leffler.hypotheses: The prescribed set has no accumulation point inside the domain.
ca.mittag-leffler.example: Prescribing simple poles with residue one at the integers leads to meromorphic partial-fraction constructions.
ca.mittag-leffler.caution: On compact Riemann surfaces analogous prescriptions have global obstructions; unrestricted plane-domain existence does not transfer.
ca.mittag-leffler.proof_idea: Correct successive finite sums by holomorphic approximants to obtain convergence on compact exhaustions.
ca.mittag-leffler.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Laurent series and isolated singularities](./notes/ca.singularities.md)
- [Montel's theorem](./notes/ca.normal.md)
ca.mittag-leffler.references:
CA: Mittag–Leffler theorem.

ra.completeness.title: Completeness of the real numbers
ra.completeness.define: Every nonempty bounded-above real set has a least upper bound.
ra.completeness.statement: Every nonempty subset of $\mathbb R$ bounded above has a least upper bound. This order completeness supports the convergence theory of real analysis.
ra.completeness.hypotheses: Work in the usual ordered field of real numbers.
ra.completeness.example: The rational numbers fail this property at the cut determined by $x^2<2$.
ra.completeness.caution: Completeness is not a consequence of the ordered-field axioms alone.
ra.completeness.prerequisites:
**From other subjects**

- [Sets, functions and relations](./notes/sl.sets.md) — Set theory and mathematical logic
ra.completeness.references:
RA2: construction and completeness of the reals.

ra.metric.title: Metric limits and completeness
ra.metric.define: A sequence is Cauchy if its tail has arbitrarily small diameter. A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges within that space.
ra.metric.statement: A sequence is Cauchy if its tail has arbitrarily small diameter. A metric space is complete when every Cauchy sequence converges within that space.
ra.metric.hypotheses: The metric, not just the topology, specifies Cauchy sequences.
ra.metric.example: $\mathbb Q$ is incomplete in the Euclidean metric; $\mathbb R$ is complete.
ra.metric.caution: Completeness does not imply compactness; bounded sequences in infinite-dimensional spaces need not have convergent subsequences.
ra.metric.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

ra.uniform.title: Uniform convergence
ra.uniform.define: Uniform convergence controls errors simultaneously at every point of the domain.
ra.uniform.statement: Uniform convergence means $\sup_{x\in X}|f_n(x)-f(x)|\to0$. A uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
ra.uniform.hypotheses: The same index bound works for every point of the domain.
ra.uniform.example: $x^n$ on $[0,1]$ converges pointwise but not uniformly.
ra.uniform.caution: Differentiation cannot generally be interchanged with a uniform limit without additional derivative control.
ra.uniform.references:
RA2: sequences of functions.

- **RA2** — Gerald B. Folland. [Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/mathematik-und-statistik/real-analysis-978-0-471-31716-6). Second edition, Wiley, 1999.

ra.ascoli.title: Arzelà–Ascoli theorem
ra.ascoli.define: On a compact metric space, a family of real or complex continuous functions is relatively compact in the uniform norm exactly when it is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.
ra.ascoli.statement: On a compact metric space, a family of real or complex continuous functions is relatively compact in the uniform norm exactly when it is equicontinuous and pointwise bounded.
ra.ascoli.hypotheses: This statement is for scalar-valued functions on a compact metric domain.
ra.ascoli.example: Uniformly bounded functions with a common Lipschitz constant satisfy the criterion.
ra.ascoli.caution: A bounded subset of a function space is not automatically relatively compact.
ra.ascoli.proof_idea: Approximate functions on finite nets and extract a diagonal subsequence; equicontinuity upgrades pointwise control to uniform control.
ra.ascoli.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Uniform convergence](./notes/ra.uniform.md)

**From other subjects**

ra.measure.title: Measure spaces
ra.measure.define: Countably additive measures assign sizes to sets in a sigma-algebra.
ra.measure.statement: A measure $\mu:\Sigma\to[0,\infty]$ is countably additive on a sigma-algebra and satisfies $\mu(\varnothing)=0$. A measurable function pulls Borel sets back into $\Sigma$.
ra.measure.hypotheses: Countable additivity applies to pairwise disjoint measurable sets.
ra.measure.example: Counting measure, Lebesgue measure and probability measures have different total masses.
ra.measure.caution: A sigma-algebra is closed under countable unions; arbitrary unions need not be measurable.
ra.measure.prerequisites:
**From other subjects**

- [Sets, functions and relations](./notes/sl.sets.md) — Set theory and mathematical logic
ra.measure.references:
RA: lectures 1–3.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.outer.title: Carathéodory extension
ra.outer.define: A premeasure on an algebra extends to a measure on the generated sigma-algebra via its induced outer measure. The extension is unique under sigma-finiteness of the premeasure.
ra.outer.statement: A premeasure on an algebra extends to a measure on the generated sigma-algebra via its induced outer measure. The extension is unique under sigma-finiteness of the premeasure.
ra.outer.hypotheses: The premeasure is countably additive whenever the disjoint union remains in the algebra.
ra.outer.example: Lengths of half-open intervals generate Lebesgue measure after extension and completion.
ra.outer.caution: Outer measure alone is only countably subadditive; measurability must be imposed.
ra.outer.proof_idea: Declare a set measurable when it splits every outer measure additively; verify countable additivity on these sets.
ra.outer.references:
RA: outer measure and measurable sets.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.integral.title: Lebesgue integration
ra.integral.define: Lebesgue integration builds integrals from measurable simple functions.
ra.integral.statement: For measurable $f\ge0$, define $\int f\,d\mu$ by suprema of integrals of simple functions below $f$. For signed or complex functions, integrability requires $\int|f|\,d\mu<\infty$.
ra.integral.hypotheses: Functions equal almost everywhere have the same integral.
ra.integral.example: The indicator of the rationals has Lebesgue integral zero on $[0,1]$ but is not Riemann integrable there.
ra.integral.caution: The expression $\infty-\infty$ is never an integral value.
ra.integral.references:
RA: definition of the Lebesgue integral.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.mct.title: Monotone convergence
ra.mct.define: Increasing nonnegative functions permit interchange of limits and integrals.
ra.mct.statement: If $0\le f_n\uparrow f$ almost everywhere, then $\int f_n\,d\mu\uparrow\int f\,d\mu$, allowing infinity.
ra.mct.hypotheses: The functions are measurable and nonnegative; no finite total measure assumption is needed.
ra.mct.example: Increasing simple approximations compute the integral of a nonnegative measurable function.
ra.mct.caution: Decreasing sequences require a finite-integral bound for the analogous conclusion.
ra.mct.proof_idea: Compare the limiting integrals with every simple function lying below the limit.
ra.mct.references:
RA: lecture 4.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.fatou.title: Fatou's lemma
ra.fatou.define: Nonnegative limits obey a one-sided inequality for their integrals.
ra.fatou.hypotheses: Nonnegativity may be replaced by a common integrable lower bound.
ra.fatou.example: Indicators of intervals $[n,n+1]$ on $\mathbb R$ show that strict inequality can occur.
ra.fatou.caution: Fatou gives an inequality, not permission to exchange integral and limit.
ra.fatou.proof_idea: Apply monotone convergence to the increasing sequence of tail infima.
ra.fatou.references:
RA: lecture 4.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.dct.title: Dominated convergence
ra.dct.define: A common integrable bound upgrades almost-everywhere convergence to convergence in mean.
ra.dct.statement: If $f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ for one $g\in L^1(\mu)$, then $f\in L^1$ and $\|f_n-f\|_1\to0$.
ra.dct.hypotheses: The dominating function is independent of $n$ and integrable on the whole domain.
ra.dct.example: $n\mathbf1_{(0,1/n)}$ has no such domination and its integrals do not approach the integral of its pointwise limit.
ra.dct.caution: Pointwise convergence plus bounded integrals alone is insufficient.
ra.dct.proof_idea: Apply Fatou to an integrable upper bound minus the absolute error.
ra.dct.references:
RA: lecture 5.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.fubini.title: Tonelli and Fubini
ra.fubini.define: On sigma-finite measure spaces, nonnegative measurable functions have equal iterated and product integrals, possibly infinite. For absolutely integrable functions, the iterated integrals agree and sections are integrable almost everywhere.
ra.fubini.statement: On sigma-finite measure spaces, nonnegative measurable functions have equal iterated and product integrals, possibly infinite. For absolutely integrable functions, the iterated integrals agree and sections are integrable almost everywhere.
ra.fubini.hypotheses: Use the product sigma-algebra; completed-measure formulations require the corresponding almost-everywhere interpretation.
ra.fubini.example: Nonnegative double series may be rearranged freely; absolutely summable signed series also may be rearranged.
ra.fubini.caution: Conditional convergence does not justify interchanging two integrals.
ra.fubini.proof_idea: Start with measurable rectangles, extend to simple functions, and then use monotone convergence; handle signed functions by absolute integrability.
ra.fubini.references:
RA: lectures 18–19.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.lp.title: Lp spaces
ra.lp.define: Lp spaces measure integrability modulo equality almost everywhere.
ra.lp.statement: For $1\le p<\infty$, $L^p(\mu)$ consists of measurable functions modulo almost-everywhere equality with norm $(\int |f|^p\,d\mu)^{1/p}$. The $L^\infty$ norm is essential supremum.
ra.lp.hypotheses: The quotient by null sets makes the norm definite.
ra.lp.example: On a finite measure space, $L^q\subseteq L^p$ when $q\ge p$.
ra.lp.caution: This inclusion need not hold on an infinite measure space; $0<p<1$ does not give a norm by this formula.
ra.lp.references:
RA: Lp spaces.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.holder.title: Hölder and Minkowski inequalities
ra.holder.define: Conjugate exponents control products, and Minkowski supplies the triangle inequality.
ra.holder.example: The case $p=q=2$ gives the integral Cauchy–Schwarz inequality.
ra.holder.caution: Endpoint cases need essential suprema; strict convexity equality statements depend on the exponent.
ra.holder.proof_idea: Use Young's inequality after normalization, then apply Hölder to the expansion controlling the pth power.
ra.holder.references:
RA: Lp inequalities.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.rn.title: Radon–Nikodym theorem
ra.rn.define: Absolute continuity of sigma-finite measures yields an almost-everywhere density.
ra.rn.statement: For sigma-finite positive measures $\nu\ll\mu$ on the same sigma-algebra, there is measurable $h\ge0$ with $\nu(A)=\int_A h\,d\mu$, unique $\mu$-almost everywhere.
ra.rn.hypotheses: Absolute continuity means every mu-null set is nu-null.
ra.rn.example: Probability densities are Radon–Nikodym derivatives relative to a chosen reference measure.
ra.rn.caution: A point mass has no density with respect to Lebesgue measure.
ra.rn.proof_idea: Construct the absolutely continuous component and use maximality to show that the residual measure vanishes.
ra.rn.references:
RA: Radon–Nikodym theorem.

ra.signed.title: Signed measures and decomposition
ra.signed.define: Finite signed measures split uniquely into mutually singular positive parts.
ra.signed.statement:
A finite signed measure has a Hahn decomposition and a unique Jordan decomposition $
u=
u^+-
u^-$ into mutually singular finite positive measures. Its total variation is $|
u|=
u^++
u^-$.
ra.signed.hypotheses: This entry restricts to finite signed measures to avoid ambiguous infinite differences.
ra.signed.example: An integrable density splits into its positive and negative parts.
ra.signed.caution: The Hahn sets are not unique as sets; the Jordan component measures are unique.
ra.signed.proof_idea: Construct positive and negative measurable regions, then restrict the measure to obtain its canonical components.
ra.signed.references:
RA: signed measures.

ra.egorov.title: Egorov and Lusin approximation
ra.egorov.define: On a finite measure space, almost-everywhere convergence is uniform outside a set of arbitrarily small measure. For a finite-valued measurable function on a finite-measure Lebesgue measurable set, restriction to a suitable compact subset is continuous with arbitrarily small measure loss.
ra.egorov.statement: On a finite measure space, almost-everywhere convergence is uniform outside a set of arbitrarily small measure. For a finite-valued measurable function on a finite-measure Lebesgue measurable set, restriction to a suitable compact subset is continuous with arbitrarily small measure loss.
ra.egorov.hypotheses: The first assertion is Egorov; the second is a Euclidean Lebesgue version of Lusin.
ra.egorov.example: Approximate a measurable function by continuous behavior after discarding a small exceptional set.
ra.egorov.caution: Neither result makes the original function globally continuous or the original convergence uniformly valid everywhere.
ra.egorov.proof_idea: Control a countable family of exceptional sets; for Lusin combine simple-function approximation with regularity.
ra.egorov.references:
RA: Egorov and Lusin theorems.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.differentiation.title: Lebesgue differentiation theorem
ra.differentiation.define: Local averages recover locally integrable functions almost everywhere.
ra.differentiation.statement: For $f\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb R^n)$, averages of $|f(y)-f(x)|$ over balls centered at $x$ tend to zero as the radius tends to zero, for almost every $x$.
ra.differentiation.hypotheses: Lebesgue measure and Euclidean balls are used here.
ra.differentiation.example: For indicators, almost every point of a measurable set is a density-one point.
ra.differentiation.caution: The conclusion is almost everywhere and cannot be extended to arbitrary metrics and measures without hypotheses.
ra.differentiation.proof_idea: Approximate locally by continuous functions and control exceptional points with a maximal inequality.
ra.differentiation.references:
RA: differentiation of integrals.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.absolute-continuity.title: Absolute continuity and the FTC
ra.absolute-continuity.define: Absolute continuity is exactly reconstruction by an integrable derivative on an interval.
ra.absolute-continuity.statement: On $[a,b]$, a function is absolutely continuous exactly when it has the form $f(x)=f(a)+\int_a^x g(t)\,dt$ for some $g\in L^1$; then $f'=g$ almost everywhere.
ra.absolute-continuity.hypotheses: The interval is compact and the derivative is interpreted almost everywhere.
ra.absolute-continuity.example: The Cantor function is continuous with derivative zero almost everywhere but is not absolutely continuous.
ra.absolute-continuity.caution: Almost-everywhere differentiability alone does not reconstruct a function from its derivative.
ra.absolute-continuity.proof_idea: Use differentiation of the indefinite integral and the measure induced by an absolutely continuous function.
ra.absolute-continuity.references:
RA: absolute continuity and differentiation.

- **RA** — Jeff Viaclovsky; notes by Ethan Brown. [MIT 18.125: Measure and Integration](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/18-125-measure-and-integration-fall-2003/pages/lecture-notes/). Fall 2003 lecture notes.

ra.fourier.title: Plancherel theorem
ra.fourier.define: The Fourier transform preserves the L2 inner product under the stated normalization.
ra.fourier.statement: With $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi ix\cdot\xi}f(x)\,dx$, the Fourier transform extends uniquely from Schwartz functions to a unitary operator on $L^2(\mathbb R^n)$.
ra.fourier.hypotheses: The extension is in the L2 norm; the integral formula need not converge pointwise for every L2 function.
ra.fourier.example: The Gaussian is mapped to a Gaussian under this convention.
ra.fourier.caution: L2 inversion is not automatically pointwise inversion.
ra.fourier.proof_idea: Prove the inner-product identity on a dense class and extend by completion.
ra.fourier.references:
RA2: Fourier analysis.

- **RA2** — Gerald B. Folland. [Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/mathematik-und-statistik/real-analysis-978-0-471-31716-6). Second edition, Wiley, 1999.

ra.distributions.title: Distributions and weak derivatives
ra.distributions.define: Test-function duality extends differentiation beyond ordinary functions.
ra.distributions.statement: A distribution on an open $U\subset\mathbb R^n$ is a continuous linear functional on $C_c^\infty(U)$ with its test-function topology. Define $\langle D^\alpha T,\phi\rangle=(-1)^{|\alpha|}\langle T,D^\alpha\phi\rangle$.
ra.distributions.hypotheses: The test-function topology controls all derivatives on a fixed compact support along convergent sequences.
ra.distributions.example: The distributional derivative of the Heaviside function is the Dirac mass.
ra.distributions.caution: A distribution need not be an ordinary function, and arbitrary distributions cannot generally be multiplied.
ra.distributions.references:
RA2: distributions and weak differentiation.

- **RA2** — Gerald B. Folland. [Real Analysis: Modern Techniques and Their Applications](https://www.wiley-vch.de/de/fachgebiete/mathematik-und-statistik/real-analysis-978-0-471-31716-6). Second edition, Wiley, 1999.

ra.sobolev.title: Sobolev spaces
ra.sobolev.define: Sobolev spaces control integrability of a function and its weak derivatives.
ra.sobolev.statement: For integer $k\ge0$ and $1\le p\le\infty$, $W^{k,p}(U)$ consists of Lp functions whose distributional derivatives of order at most k also lie in Lp.
ra.sobolev.hypotheses: Representatives are identified almost everywhere; the domain is open.
ra.sobolev.example: $W^{1,2}$ is the natural energy space for many elliptic equations.
ra.sobolev.caution: Boundary traces and compact embeddings require extra domain and exponent assumptions.

fa.banach.title: Banach spaces
fa.banach.define: A Banach space is a normed real or complex vector space complete for its norm metric.
fa.banach.statement: A Banach space is a normed real or complex vector space complete for its norm metric.
fa.banach.hypotheses: The scalar field and norm must be specified.
fa.banach.example: $L^p(\mu)$ is Banach for $1\le p\le\infty$; $C(K)$ is Banach with the sup norm for compact K.
fa.banach.caution: A linear subspace of a Banach space is complete in the inherited norm exactly when it is closed.
fa.banach.prerequisites:

fa.hilbert.title: Hilbert spaces and orthogonal projection
fa.hilbert.define: A Hilbert space is complete in its inner-product norm. Every vector has a unique orthogonal decomposition relative to a closed linear subspace.
fa.hilbert.statement: A Hilbert space is complete in its inner-product norm. Every vector has a unique orthogonal decomposition relative to a closed linear subspace.
fa.hilbert.hypotheses: The subspace must be closed; use real or complex inner products consistently.
fa.hilbert.example: Least-squares approximation projects onto a finite-dimensional span.
fa.hilbert.caution: Projection onto a nonclosed subspace may fail to exist.
fa.hilbert.proof_idea: Minimize distance using the parallelogram identity to make a minimizing sequence Cauchy.
fa.hilbert.references:

fa.operators.title: Bounded linear operators
fa.operators.define: Continuity of a linear map is equivalent to a uniform norm bound.
fa.operators.statement: A linear map $T:X\to Y$ between normed spaces is bounded if $\|Tx\|\le C\|x\|$. This is equivalent to continuity. Its operator norm is $\sup_{\|x\|\le1}\|Tx\|$.
fa.operators.hypotheses: Boundedness is a global linear estimate.
fa.operators.example: Differentiation is bounded from C1 with its C1 norm to C with its sup norm, but not with only the sup norm on the domain.
fa.operators.caution: An operator's boundedness depends on its domain and the chosen norms.
fa.operators.references:
FA: bounded operators.

fa.dual.title: Continuous dual and bidual
fa.dual.define: The continuous dual records bounded linear measurements of a normed space.
fa.dual.statement: The continuous dual $X^*$ consists of bounded linear scalar-valued functionals. The canonical map $J:X\to X^{**}$ is given by $Jx(\ell)=\ell(x)$ and is isometric.
fa.dual.hypotheses: Use the continuous dual rather than the algebraic dual.
fa.dual.example: For $1<p<\infty$ on a sigma-finite measure space, $(L^p)^*$ is identified with $L^q$ by integration.
fa.dual.caution: The full dual of $L^\infty$ generally exceeds $L^1$.
fa.dual.prerequisites:

fa.hahn-banach.title: Hahn–Banach extension theorem
fa.hahn-banach.define: A bounded linear functional on a linear subspace of a normed space extends to the entire space with unchanged norm.
fa.hahn-banach.statement: A bounded linear functional on a linear subspace of a normed space extends to the entire space with unchanged norm.
fa.hahn-banach.hypotheses: The extension is scalar-valued; the real sublinear-domination version yields the complex normed-space statement as well.
fa.hahn-banach.example: A nonzero vector can be separated from zero by a norm-one continuous functional.
fa.hahn-banach.caution: Arbitrary vector-valued operators need not admit norm-preserving extensions.
fa.hahn-banach.proof_idea: Extend one dimension at a time under a domination bound and use a maximal extension argument.

fa.baire.title: Baire category theorem
fa.baire.define: A nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets. Equivalently, countable intersections of dense open sets are dense.
fa.baire.statement: A nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of nowhere dense sets. Equivalently, countable intersections of dense open sets are dense.
fa.baire.hypotheses: Completeness is a sufficient hypothesis; locally compact Hausdorff spaces are another important version.
fa.baire.example: This underlies the uniform boundedness and open mapping principles.
fa.baire.caution: Meagre and measure-zero are different notions of smallness.
fa.baire.proof_idea: Choose nested closed balls avoiding successive nowhere dense sets; completeness supplies a common point.
fa.baire.prerequisites:
**From other subjects**

- [Metric limits and completeness](./notes/ra.metric.md) — Real analysis
fa.baire.references:

fa.uniform-boundedness.title: Uniform boundedness principle
fa.uniform-boundedness.define: Pointwise bounded operator families on a Banach domain have uniformly bounded norms.
fa.uniform-boundedness.statement: If X is Banach and $\{T_i:X\to Y\}$ are bounded linear maps with $\sup_i\|T_i x\|<\infty$ for each x, then $\sup_i\|T_i\|<\infty$.
fa.uniform-boundedness.hypotheses: Y need only be normed; the completeness requirement is on X.
fa.uniform-boundedness.example: Pointwise bounded continuous linear functionals on a Banach space have uniformly bounded norms.
fa.uniform-boundedness.caution: Pointwise boundedness on a merely dense set is not enough.
fa.uniform-boundedness.proof_idea: Apply Baire to closed sets on which all operator values have a common bound, then translate and rescale a ball.
fa.uniform-boundedness.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

fa.open-mapping.title: Open mapping and bounded inverse
fa.open-mapping.define: A surjective bounded linear map between Banach spaces is open. A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces therefore has bounded inverse.
fa.open-mapping.statement: A surjective bounded linear map between Banach spaces is open. A bounded linear bijection between Banach spaces therefore has bounded inverse.
fa.open-mapping.hypotheses: Both spaces are complete, and surjectivity is required for openness.
fa.open-mapping.example: Equivalent Banach norms can be proved equivalent by the bounded inverse theorem when the identity map is a bounded bijection.
fa.open-mapping.caution: An algebraic inverse need not be continuous when completeness fails.
fa.open-mapping.proof_idea: Baire gives a ball in the closure of an image; a convergent correction series upgrades closure to actual inclusion.
fa.open-mapping.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

fa.closed-graph.title: Closed graph theorem
fa.closed-graph.define: An everywhere-defined linear map between Banach spaces is bounded if and only if its graph is closed in the product space.
fa.closed-graph.statement: An everywhere-defined linear map between Banach spaces is bounded if and only if its graph is closed in the product space.
fa.closed-graph.hypotheses: The map is defined on all of X; X and Y are Banach.
fa.closed-graph.example: A closed differential operator may be unbounded when its domain is only a dense proper subspace.
fa.closed-graph.caution: Closedness of a densely defined operator alone does not imply boundedness.
fa.closed-graph.proof_idea: View the graph as a Banach space and apply the bounded inverse theorem to its projection onto X.
fa.closed-graph.prerequisites:

fa.weak.title: Weak and weak-star topologies
fa.weak.define: Weak and weak-star topologies test convergence against different families of functionals.
fa.weak.statement: Weak convergence in X means convergence against every element of $X^*$. Weak-star convergence in $X^*$ means pointwise convergence on X.
fa.weak.hypotheses: The specified predual determines the weak-star topology.
fa.weak.example: An orthonormal sequence in a Hilbert space converges weakly to zero but not in norm.
fa.weak.caution: Weak and weak-star topologies generally differ; their compactness is naturally formulated using nets, not only sequences.
fa.weak.references:
FA2: weak topologies.

fa.alaoglu.title: Banach–Alaoglu theorem
fa.alaoglu.define: A dual unit ball is compact for the weak-star topology.
fa.alaoglu.statement: The closed unit ball of $X^*$ is compact in the weak-star topology for every normed space X.
fa.alaoglu.hypotheses: Weak-star compactness is not norm compactness.
fa.alaoglu.example: If X is separable, this weak-star compact ball is metrizable and hence sequentially compact.
fa.alaoglu.caution: Without metrizability, compactness does not automatically imply sequential compactness.
fa.alaoglu.proof_idea: Embed the dual ball into a product of compact scalar disks and verify that the functional conditions define a closed subset.

fa.reflexive.title: Reflexive spaces
fa.reflexive.define: Reflexivity identifies a Banach space with its bidual and gives weak ball compactness.
fa.reflexive.statement: A Banach space X is reflexive when $J:X\to X^{**}$ is onto. This is equivalent to weak compactness of its closed unit ball.
fa.reflexive.hypotheses: Weak topology is the topology induced by the continuous dual.
fa.reflexive.example: Hilbert spaces and $L^p$ for $1<p<\infty$ are reflexive.
fa.reflexive.caution: $L^1([0,1])$ and $L^\infty([0,1])$ with Lebesgue measure are not reflexive.
fa.reflexive.proof_idea: For reflexive spaces identify the ball with a weak-star compact bidual ball; the converse uses separation and density of the canonical image.
fa.reflexive.references:

fa.riesz.title: Riesz representation in Hilbert space
fa.riesz.define: Every continuous Hilbert-space functional is inner product with a unique vector.
fa.riesz.statement: With inner product linear in the first variable, every continuous linear functional on H has the unique form $x\mapsto\langle x,y\rangle$ for some y, with norm $\|y\|$.
fa.riesz.hypotheses: H is a Hilbert space; the convention fixes the conjugate-linearity of the representing correspondence.
fa.riesz.example: Coordinate evaluation on $\ell^2$ is represented by a standard basis vector.
fa.riesz.caution: This is distinct from the Riesz–Markov theorem representing functionals by measures.
fa.riesz.proof_idea: Project onto the orthogonal complement of the functional's kernel.

fa.compact.title: Compact operators
fa.compact.define: A bounded operator is compact if it sends the unit ball to a relatively norm-compact set.
fa.compact.statement: A bounded operator is compact if it sends the unit ball to a relatively norm-compact set.
fa.compact.hypotheses: The domain and codomain are normed; the standard operator theory below uses Banach spaces.
fa.compact.example: Finite-rank operators are compact, and their operator-norm limits into a Banach space are compact.
fa.compact.caution: The identity on an infinite-dimensional Banach space is not compact.

fa.fredholm.title: Fredholm alternative for I minus compact
fa.fredholm.define: Identity minus a compact operator has equivalent injectivity and surjectivity.
fa.fredholm.statement: For compact K on a Banach space X, $I-K$ is injective if and only if it is surjective. Its kernel is finite-dimensional and its range is closed.
fa.fredholm.hypotheses: The operator has the particular form identity minus a compact operator.
fa.fredholm.example: A second-kind integral equation has either unique solvability for every right-hand side or a nontrivial homogeneous solution.
fa.fredholm.caution: For a nontrivial kernel, solvability still requires compatibility conditions; arbitrary bounded operators need not satisfy this alternative.
fa.fredholm.proof_idea: Compactness prevents infinite separated sequences in successive kernels or ranges.

fa.spectrum.title: Spectrum and resolvent
fa.spectrum.define: The spectrum records failure of a bounded everywhere-defined inverse.
fa.spectrum.statement: For a bounded operator T on a complex Banach space, $\sigma(T)$ consists of scalars for which $T-\lambda I$ has no bounded everywhere-defined inverse. It is nonempty and compact.
fa.spectrum.hypotheses: Nonemptiness uses the complex scalar field and a nonzero Banach space.
fa.spectrum.example: The unilateral shift has spectral points that are not eigenvalues.
fa.spectrum.caution: In infinite dimensions, spectrum and set of eigenvalues are not the same.
fa.spectrum.prerequisites:

fa.compact-spectral.title: Compact self-adjoint spectral theorem
fa.compact-spectral.define: A compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has orthogonal finite-dimensional eigenspaces for its nonzero eigenvalues; those eigenvalues can accumulate only at zero. The closed span of these eigenspaces is the orthogonal complement of the kernel.
fa.compact-spectral.statement: A compact self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space has orthogonal finite-dimensional eigenspaces for its nonzero eigenvalues; those eigenvalues can accumulate only at zero. The closed span of these eigenspaces is the orthogonal complement of the kernel.
fa.compact-spectral.hypotheses: Self-adjointness and compactness are both assumed.
fa.compact-spectral.example: A diagonal operator on l2 with real diagonal entries tending to zero is compact and self-adjoint.
fa.compact-spectral.caution: A kernel may be infinite-dimensional; zero need not be an eigenvalue when it is a spectral limit point.
fa.compact-spectral.proof_idea: Maximize the quadratic form to obtain an eigenvector, then iterate on orthogonal complements.

fa.spectral-measure.title: Spectral theorem for bounded normal operators
fa.spectral-measure.define: Bounded normal operators have a projection-valued spectral representation.
fa.spectral-measure.statement: A bounded normal operator on a complex Hilbert space admits a projection-valued measure E with $T=\int_{\sigma(T)}z\,dE(z)$ and a bounded Borel functional calculus.
fa.spectral-measure.example: Multiplication by the coordinate function on L2 can have continuous spectrum without an eigenbasis.

fa.spectral-measure.proof_idea: Represent the commutative operator algebra by continuous functions and then extend the calculus to spectral projections.

fa.unbounded.title: Unbounded self-adjoint operators
fa.unbounded.define: Self-adjointness of an unbounded operator includes equality of operator domains.
fa.unbounded.statement: A densely defined operator A is self-adjoint when $A=A^*$ including equality of domains. Such operators have real spectrum and a spectral calculus respecting domains.
fa.unbounded.hypotheses: Specify the dense domain and adjoint domain, not just a formal expression.
fa.unbounded.example: Different boundary conditions for a differential expression can produce different self-adjoint operators.
fa.unbounded.caution: A symmetric operator need not be self-adjoint or essentially self-adjoint.

fa.lax-milgram.title: Lax–Milgram theorem
fa.lax-milgram.define: Bounded coercive forms give unique variational solutions with a norm estimate.
fa.lax-milgram.statement: A bounded coercive sesquilinear form a on a Hilbert space yields a unique solution u to $a(u,v)=\ell(v)$ for every continuous antilinear functional $\ell$, with $\|u\|\le\|\ell\|/\alpha$.
fa.lax-milgram.hypotheses: The form is linear in its first variable and $\operatorname{Re}a(v,v)\ge\alpha\|v\|^2$ for some $\alpha>0$.
fa.lax-milgram.example: The weak Dirichlet problem for the coercive form integral of gradient products is a model application on H1_0 with an appropriate norm.
fa.lax-milgram.caution: Positivity without a uniform coercivity bound is insufficient.
fa.lax-milgram.proof_idea: Represent the form by a bounded operator, use coercivity for closed range and an adjoint argument for density.

gt.groups.title: Groups and homomorphisms
gt.groups.define: A group is a set with an associative multiplication, an identity and inverses. A homomorphism preserves multiplication and therefore identities and inverses.
gt.groups.statement: A group is a set with an associative multiplication, an identity and inverses. A homomorphism preserves multiplication and therefore identities and inverses.
gt.groups.hypotheses: Commutativity is an additional condition, not part of the group axioms.
gt.groups.example: $S_n$, invertible matrices, and the additive integers are basic examples.
gt.groups.caution: A set of symmetries must be closed under composition and inverse to form a group.
gt.groups.prerequisites:

gt.subgroups.title: Subgroups and generated subgroups
gt.subgroups.define: Subgroups inherit the operation; generators specify the smallest containing subgroup.
gt.subgroups.statement: A nonempty subset H of G is a subgroup when $xy^{-1}\in H$ for all x,y in H. The subgroup generated by S is the intersection of subgroups containing S.
gt.subgroups.hypotheses: The ambient group operation is inherited.
gt.subgroups.example: Every subgroup of the additive integers is $n\mathbb Z$ for a unique $n\ge0$.
gt.subgroups.caution: Closure under multiplication alone need not suffice for an infinite subset.
gt.subgroups.references:
GT: subgroups.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.lagrange.title: Cosets and Lagrange's theorem
gt.lagrange.define: Cosets partition a finite group into equal-sized pieces.
gt.lagrange.statement: The left cosets of H partition G. If G is finite, $|G|=[G:H]|H|$, so subgroup orders and element orders divide $|G|$.
gt.lagrange.hypotheses: The divisibility statement is for finite groups.
gt.lagrange.example: A group of prime order is cyclic.
gt.lagrange.caution: A divisor of the group order need not be the order of a subgroup.
gt.lagrange.proof_idea: Each coset is in bijection with H by translation, and distinct cosets are disjoint.
gt.lagrange.references:
GT: cosets.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.quotients.title: Normal subgroups and quotients
gt.quotients.define: Normality makes multiplication on cosets independent of representatives.
gt.quotients.statement: A subgroup N is normal when $gNg^{-1}=N$ for every g. Then multiplication of cosets makes $G/N$ a group, and N is the kernel of the quotient map.
gt.quotients.hypotheses: Normality ensures that coset multiplication is independent of representatives.
gt.quotients.caution: A coset set by a nonnormal subgroup is generally not a quotient group.
gt.quotients.references:
GT: kernels and quotients.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.isomorphism.title: First isomorphism theorem
gt.isomorphism.define: Quotienting a homomorphism's domain by its kernel recovers its image.
gt.isomorphism.statement: For a group homomorphism $\phi:G\to H$, the induced map $G/\ker\phi\to\operatorname{im}\phi$ is an isomorphism.
gt.isomorphism.hypotheses: Surjectivity onto H is unnecessary if the target is restricted to the image.
gt.isomorphism.example: The determinant identifies GLn modulo SLn with the nonzero scalars.
gt.isomorphism.caution: The theorem identifies the quotient with the image, not automatically with all of H.
gt.isomorphism.proof_idea: Send a coset of the kernel to the common image of its representatives and check injectivity and surjectivity.
gt.isomorphism.references:
GT: homomorphism theorems.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.actions.title: Group actions
gt.actions.define: Actions represent group elements as compatible permutations of a set.
gt.actions.statement: An action of G on X is a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{Sym}(X)$. Orbits partition X and stabilizers are subgroups.
gt.actions.hypotheses: Specify left or right actions and use one convention consistently.
gt.actions.example: Conjugation is an action of a group on itself; its stabilizers are centralizers.
gt.actions.caution: Faithful and transitive describe different properties.
gt.actions.references:
GT: groups acting on sets.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.orbit-stabilizer.title: Orbit–stabilizer theorem
gt.orbit-stabilizer.define: An orbit is identified with the cosets of a point stabilizer.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.statement: For x in a G-set, the map $G/G_x\to Gx$ is a bijection. If G is finite, $|Gx|=|G|/|G_x|$.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.hypotheses: The quotient here is a coset set; the stabilizer need not be normal.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.example: Counting a polygon's vertex orbit determines the size of its vertex stabilizer.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.caution: Transitivity does not imply that the action is free.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.proof_idea: Two group elements send x to the same point exactly when they lie in the same stabilizer coset.
gt.orbit-stabilizer.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Group actions](./notes/gt.actions.md)
- [Cosets and Lagrange's theorem](./notes/gt.lagrange.md)
gt.orbit-stabilizer.references:
GT: orbit and stabilizer.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.class-equation.title: Class equation and finite p-groups
gt.class-equation.define: Conjugacy-class counting forces nontrivial centers in finite prime-power groups.
gt.class-equation.statement: A finite group decomposes as $|G|=|Z(G)|+\sum [G:C_G(x_i)]$, summing over noncentral conjugacy classes. A nontrivial finite p-group has nontrivial center.
gt.class-equation.hypotheses: The p-group conclusion assumes the group order is a positive power of a prime.
gt.class-equation.example: Every group of order p squared is abelian.
gt.class-equation.caution: A nontrivial center does not by itself make a group abelian.
gt.class-equation.proof_idea: Apply orbit–stabilizer to conjugation and reduce the class equation modulo p.
gt.class-equation.references:
GT: conjugation actions.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.sylow.title: Sylow theorems
gt.sylow.define: Prime-power subgroups obey existence, conjugacy and counting constraints.
gt.sylow.statement: If $|G|=p^a m$ with $p\nmid m$, subgroups of order $p^a$ exist, every p-subgroup is contained in one, all such maximal p-subgroups are conjugate, and their number divides m and is $1\bmod p$.
gt.sylow.hypotheses: G is finite and p is prime.
gt.sylow.example: A unique Sylow p-subgroup is normal.
gt.sylow.caution: The congruence and divisibility constraints may not uniquely determine the number of Sylow subgroups.
gt.sylow.proof_idea: Use group actions on subsets or cosets to force fixed points and conjugacy.
gt.sylow.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Orbit–stabilizer theorem](./notes/gt.orbit-stabilizer.md)
- [Class equation and finite p-groups](./notes/gt.class-equation.md)

gt.products.title: Direct products
gt.products.define: The direct product of groups has componentwise multiplication. Internally, commuting normal subgroups with trivial intersection and product G realize G as their direct product.
gt.products.statement: The direct product of groups has componentwise multiplication. Internally, commuting normal subgroups with trivial intersection and product G realize G as their direct product.
gt.products.hypotheses: For the internal two-factor statement, both subgroups are normal and their intersection is trivial.
gt.products.example: $C_2\times C_2$ is not cyclic, whereas $C_2\times C_3\cong C_6$.
gt.products.caution: Orders alone do not determine a direct-product decomposition.
gt.products.references:
GT: direct products.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.semidirect.title: Semidirect products and split extensions
gt.semidirect.define: An action assembles two groups into a split extension.
gt.semidirect.hypotheses: The action by automorphisms is part of the data.
gt.semidirect.example: Dihedral groups combine rotations with a reflection acting by inversion.
gt.semidirect.caution: A short exact sequence need not split; a normal subgroup and quotient do not determine the extension.
gt.semidirect.references:
GT: automorphisms and extensions.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.presentations.title: Free groups and presentations
gt.presentations.define: Generators and relations express a group as a quotient of a free group.
gt.presentations.statement: The free group F(S) realizes arbitrary maps from S into groups uniquely as homomorphisms. A presentation $\langle S\mid R\rangle$ means $F(S)$ modulo the normal closure of R.
gt.presentations.hypotheses: Relations are imposed normally, so all conjugates are also identified with the identity.
gt.presentations.example: $\langle a\mid a^n=1\rangle$ presents a cyclic group of order n.
gt.presentations.caution: Finite presentations do not guarantee an effective general solution of the word problem.
gt.presentations.references:
GT: free groups and presentations.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.solvable.title: Derived series and solvable groups
gt.solvable.define: Repeated commutators eventually vanish in a solvable group.
gt.solvable.statement: The derived series is $G^{(0)}=G$, $G^{(i+1)}=[G^{(i)},G^{(i)}]$. A group is solvable if this reaches the identity after finitely many steps.
gt.solvable.hypotheses: Commutator subgroups measure failure of commutativity.
gt.solvable.caution: Solvable does not mean abelian, and finite groups are not all solvable.
gt.solvable.references:
GT: solvable groups.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.nilpotent.title: Central series and nilpotent groups
gt.nilpotent.define: Nilpotence requires termination of the lower central series.
gt.nilpotent.statement: A group is nilpotent when its lower central series $\gamma_1(G)=G$, $\gamma_{i+1}(G)=[G,\gamma_i(G)]$ reaches the identity.
gt.nilpotent.hypotheses: This is finite-step nilpotence, not local nilpotence.
gt.nilpotent.example: Every finite p-group is nilpotent; S3 is solvable but not nilpotent.
gt.nilpotent.caution: Nilpotence implies solvability, but the converse fails.

gt.jordan-holder.title: Jordan–Hölder theorem
gt.jordan-holder.define: Any two composition series of a finite group have the same simple factors up to isomorphism and permutation.
gt.jordan-holder.statement: Any two composition series of a finite group have the same simple factors up to isomorphism and permutation.
gt.jordan-holder.hypotheses: A composition series has simple successive quotients and strictly descending subgroups.
gt.jordan-holder.example: Composition factors are structural invariants even when a group has different composition series.
gt.jordan-holder.caution: The factors do not determine the group: extension data remain.
gt.jordan-holder.proof_idea: Refine and compare series using the isomorphism theorems and a refinement argument.

gt.abelian-structure.title: Finitely generated abelian groups
gt.abelian-structure.define: A finitely generated abelian group splits into free and finite cyclic factors.
gt.abelian-structure.statement: Every finitely generated abelian group is $\mathbb Z^r\oplus\mathbb Z/d_1\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathbb Z/d_k$ with $1<d_1\mid\cdots\mid d_k$; the rank and invariant factors are unique.
gt.abelian-structure.hypotheses: Finite generation is essential to this classification.
gt.abelian-structure.example: $\mathbb Z\oplus\mathbb Z/12$ combines a free part and torsion.
gt.abelian-structure.caution: The additive rational group is not covered by this finite-generation theorem.
gt.abelian-structure.proof_idea: Apply Smith normal form to a finite relation matrix over the integers.
gt.abelian-structure.references:
GT: commutative groups.

gt.representations.title: Linear representations
gt.representations.define: Linear representations realize a group by invertible linear transformations.
gt.representations.statement: A representation is a homomorphism $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$, equivalently a module over the group algebra. It is irreducible when V has no nonzero proper invariant subspace.
gt.representations.hypotheses: Fix the scalar field and whether the representation is finite-dimensional.
gt.representations.example: The regular representation acts by translation on a basis indexed by G.
gt.representations.references:
GT: representations of finite groups.

- **GT** — J. S. Milne. [Group Theory](https://www.jmilne.org/math/CourseNotes/GT.pdf). Version 4.01, 2025.

gt.maschke.title: Maschke's theorem
gt.maschke.define: Finite-group representations split into irreducibles when the group order is invertible.
gt.maschke.statement: If G is finite and the characteristic of k does not divide $|G|$, every finite-dimensional k-representation of G is a direct sum of irreducibles.
gt.maschke.hypotheses: The group order must be invertible in the field.
gt.maschke.example: Over the complex numbers, finite-group representations are completely reducible.
gt.maschke.caution: In characteristic p for a group of order divisible by p, invariant complements can fail.
gt.maschke.proof_idea: Average any projection onto an invariant subspace over the group to obtain an equivariant projection.
gt.maschke.references:

gt.characters.title: Characters and orthogonality
gt.characters.define: Irreducible complex characters form an orthonormal basis of class functions.
gt.characters.statement: For finite G over $\mathbb C$, irreducible characters form an orthonormal basis of class functions for $\langle\chi,\psi\rangle=|G|^{-1}\sum_g\chi(g)\overline{\psi(g)}$.
gt.characters.hypotheses: Characters are traces of finite-dimensional representations; the inner product is over all group elements.
gt.characters.example: Character inner products compute multiplicities in a representation.
gt.characters.caution: This ordinary-character statement does not transfer unchanged to modular representation theory.
gt.characters.proof_idea: Average intertwining maps and apply Schur's lemma.

gt.galois.title: Finite Galois correspondence
gt.galois.define: Finite Galois extensions reverse the inclusions between subfields and subgroups.
gt.galois.statement: For a finite Galois extension L/K, intermediate fields E correspond inclusion-reversingly to subgroups of $\operatorname{Gal}(L/K)$. Normal subgroups correspond to extensions E/K that are Galois.
gt.galois.hypotheses: The extension must be finite, normal and separable.
gt.galois.example: The splitting field of $x^3-2$ over $\mathbb Q$ has group $S_3$.
gt.galois.caution: An arbitrary finite field extension does not satisfy this subgroup–subfield correspondence in the same form.
gt.galois.proof_idea: Use fixed fields and independence of field embeddings to identify subgroup indices with field degrees.

nt.divisibility.title: Euclidean algorithm and unique factorization
nt.divisibility.define: The Euclidean algorithm underlies Bezout identities and unique integer factorization.
nt.divisibility.statement: Every integer greater than one factors uniquely into primes up to order. For integers a,b not both zero, their positive gcd is $ua+vb$ for some integers u,v.
nt.divisibility.hypotheses: Factorization is in the ordinary integers.
nt.divisibility.caution: Unique factorization of elements may fail in rings of algebraic integers.
nt.divisibility.proof_idea: The Euclidean algorithm gives Bezout's identity; Euclid's lemma then proves uniqueness by induction.

nt.crt.title: Chinese remainder theorem
nt.crt.define: Coprime congruence conditions combine into one unique residue class.
nt.crt.statement: For pairwise coprime positive integers $m_i$, $\mathbb Z/(\prod m_i)\cong\prod_i\mathbb Z/m_i$ as rings via the residue map.
nt.crt.hypotheses: Pairwise coprimality permits arbitrary independent residues.
nt.crt.caution: Without coprimality, residues must satisfy compatibility conditions.
nt.crt.proof_idea: Bezout coefficients construct idempotents selecting each coordinate.
nt.crt.references:
NT: Chinese remainder theorem.

nt.finite-fields.title: Finite fields
nt.finite-fields.define: Finite fields exist uniquely at prime-power sizes and have cyclic unit groups.
nt.finite-fields.statement: A finite field has $p^n$ elements. For each prime p and positive n there is exactly one up to isomorphism, the splitting field of $x^{p^n}-x$ over $\mathbb F_p$. Its multiplicative group is cyclic.
nt.finite-fields.hypotheses: Cardinality must be a prime power.
nt.finite-fields.caution: $\mathbb Z/4\mathbb Z$ is not a field.
nt.finite-fields.proof_idea: Frobenius identifies the roots as a field; root bounds for polynomials prove multiplicative cyclicity.

nt.reciprocity.title: Quadratic reciprocity
nt.reciprocity.define: Quadratic reciprocity relates square residues modulo two odd primes.
nt.reciprocity.statement: For distinct odd primes p,q, $(\frac pq)(\frac qp)=(-1)^{(p-1)(q-1)/4}$. Also $(\frac{-1}p)=(-1)^{(p-1)/2}$ and $(\frac2p)=(-1)^{(p^2-1)/8}$.
nt.reciprocity.hypotheses: The Legendre symbol is 1 for a nonzero square, -1 for a nonsquare, and 0 for a multiple of p.
nt.reciprocity.caution: A Jacobi symbol of one does not certify a square modulo a composite integer.
nt.reciprocity.proof_idea: Gauss's lemma turns the symbols into parity counts of lattice points.
nt.reciprocity.references:
NT2: quadratic reciprocity.

nt.number-fields.title: Number fields, norm and trace
nt.number-fields.define: Finite rational extensions carry field norms, traces and complex embeddings.
nt.number-fields.statement: A number field is a finite extension K of $\mathbb Q$. The determinant and trace of multiplication by a define $N_{K/\mathbb Q}(a)$ and $\operatorname{Tr}_{K/\mathbb Q}(a)$.
nt.number-fields.hypotheses: Characteristic zero ensures separability; the degree counts complex embeddings.
nt.number-fields.caution: Field norm is multiplicative, not a metric-space norm.

nt.integers.title: Algebraic integers
nt.integers.define: Monic integer equations single out the integral arithmetic inside a number field.
nt.integers.statement: An element integral over $\mathbb Z$ satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients. The integers of K form a ring $\mathcal O_K$, free of rank $[K:\mathbb Q]$ over $\mathbb Z$.
nt.integers.hypotheses: K is a number field; a rational algebraic integer is an integer.
nt.integers.caution: A field generator need not generate its entire ring of integers.

nt.discriminant.title: Trace pairing and discriminants
nt.discriminant.define: The trace pairing defines an arithmetic invariant of an integral basis.
nt.discriminant.statement: A basis $\omega_i$ has discriminant $\det(\operatorname{Tr}(\omega_i\omega_j))$. An integral basis defines the basis-independent field discriminant $d_K$.
nt.discriminant.hypotheses: A suborder's discriminant is the field discriminant times the square of its index.
nt.discriminant.caution: Polynomial and field discriminants can differ.

nt.ideals.title: Dedekind domains and ideal factorization
nt.ideals.define: The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain. Every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into nonzero prime ideals.
nt.ideals.statement: The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain. Every nonzero proper ideal factors uniquely into nonzero prime ideals.
nt.ideals.hypotheses: Dedekind here means Noetherian, integrally closed and dimension one.
nt.ideals.example: $\mathbb Z[\sqrt{-5}]$ has unique ideal factorization despite nonunique element factorization.
nt.ideals.caution: Unique ideal factorization does not imply every ideal is principal.

nt.class-group.title: Ideal class group
nt.class-group.define: Ideal classes measure the obstruction to principal ideal factorization.
nt.class-group.statement: The group of nonzero fractional ideals modulo principal fractional ideals is $\operatorname{Cl}(K)$. It is trivial exactly when $\mathcal O_K$ is a PID, equivalently a UFD.
nt.class-group.hypotheses: Fractional ideals are invertible in a Dedekind domain.

nt.minkowski.title: Minkowski's theorem and finite class number
nt.minkowski.define: Large symmetric convex bodies contain lattice points, bounding ideal class representatives.
nt.minkowski.statement: A centrally symmetric convex measurable body in $\mathbb R^n$ of volume greater than $2^n\operatorname{covol}(\Lambda)$ contains a nonzero point of the full lattice $\Lambda$. This implies finiteness of $\operatorname{Cl}(K)$.
nt.minkowski.hypotheses: Strict inequality avoids boundary subtleties for nonclosed bodies.
nt.minkowski.example: Real and complex embeddings of ideals produce explicit bounds for ideal class representatives.
nt.minkowski.caution: Convexity and central symmetry are essential to this formulation.
nt.minkowski.proof_idea: Apply a lattice pigeonhole argument to half the body, then bound norms in inverse ideal classes.

nt.units.title: Dirichlet's unit theorem
nt.units.define: The unit group has a finite torsion part and a rank determined by embeddings.
nt.units.statement: If K has $r_1$ real embeddings and $r_2$ conjugate pairs of complex embeddings, $\mathcal O_K^\times\cong\mu_K\times\mathbb Z^{r_1+r_2-1}$.
nt.units.hypotheses: The finite group of roots of unity is the torsion subgroup.
nt.units.caution: Computing fundamental units is a separate problem from determining their rank.
nt.units.proof_idea: The logarithmic embedding and geometry of numbers yield a full lattice in a hyperplane.

nt.padic.title: p-adic numbers and Hensel lifting
nt.padic.define: Prime-adic completion supports lifting simple polynomial roots to exact roots.
nt.padic.statement: Complete $\mathbb Q$ for $|x|_p=p^{-v_p(x)}$ to obtain $\mathbb Q_p$. If $f\in\mathbb Z_p[x]$, $f(a)\equiv0\pmod p$ and $f'(a)\not\equiv0\pmod p$, f has a unique root congruent to a modulo p in $\mathbb Z_p$.
nt.padic.hypotheses: This is the simple-root form of Hensel's lemma.
nt.padic.example: $x^2-2$ has a root in $\mathbb Z_7$ lifting 3 modulo 7.
nt.padic.caution: A multiple root modulo p need not lift by this criterion.
nt.padic.proof_idea: Newton iteration improves the p-adic error and converges by completeness.

nt.ramification.title: Splitting and ramification
nt.ramification.define: Prime ideals describe splitting, residue degrees and ramification of rational primes.
nt.ramification.statement: In $\mathcal O_K$, $p\mathcal O_K=\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^{e_i}$ with residue degrees $f_i$ and $\sum_i e_if_i=[K:\mathbb Q]$. A rational prime ramifies exactly when it divides $d_K$.
nt.ramification.hypotheses: Use the full ring of integers of a number field.
nt.ramification.caution: Factoring a defining polynomial can mislead at primes dividing the index of the chosen order.
nt.ramification.proof_idea: Compare residue-field dimensions and detect ramification through the trace pairing.

nt.zeta.title: Riemann zeta function
nt.zeta.define: The zeta function connects integer summation with an Euler product over primes.
nt.zeta.statement: For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $\zeta(s)=\sum_{n\ge1}n^{-s}=\prod_p(1-p^{-s})^{-1}$. It extends meromorphically to the plane with only a simple pole at 1, of residue one.
nt.zeta.hypotheses: Absolute convergence of the series and product holds in the stated half-plane.
nt.zeta.example: The logarithmic derivative encodes prime powers.
nt.zeta.caution: Continuation does not justify using a divergent Euler product term by term.
nt.zeta.proof_idea: Unique factorization gives the product; integral representations provide continuation.
nt.zeta.prerequisites:
