nt.dirichlet-characters.title: Dirichlet characters and L-functions
nt.dirichlet-characters.define: Multiplicative characters separate residue classes through their L-functions.
nt.dirichlet-characters.statement: A character modulo q is a character of $(\mathbb Z/q\mathbb Z)^\times$, extended by zero on nonunits. For $\operatorname{Re}s>1$, $L(s,\chi)=\sum_{n\ge1}\chi(n)n^{-s}$.
nt.dirichlet-characters.hypotheses: Distinguish primitive characters from characters induced from smaller moduli.
nt.dirichlet-characters.example: Character orthogonality isolates reduced residue classes.
nt.dirichlet-characters.caution: The principal character has Euler factors removed at primes dividing q.

nt.dirichlet.title: Dirichlet's theorem on primes
nt.dirichlet.define: Every residue class coprime to its modulus contains infinitely many primes.
nt.dirichlet.statement: If $\gcd(a,q)=1$ and $q\ge1$, infinitely many primes satisfy $p\equiv a\pmod q$.
nt.dirichlet.hypotheses: The residue class is coprime to the modulus.
nt.dirichlet.example: There are infinitely many primes congruent to 3 modulo 4.
nt.dirichlet.caution: Infinitude alone supplies no asymptotic count.
nt.dirichlet.proof_idea: Use character orthogonality and nonvanishing of nonprincipal L-functions at one.

nt.pnt.title: Prime number theorem
nt.pnt.define: The counting function of primes has a logarithmic asymptotic density.
nt.pnt.statement: If $\pi(x)$ counts primes at most x, then $\pi(x)\sim x/\log x$ as $x\to\infty$.
nt.pnt.hypotheses: The logarithm is natural; no error term is claimed here.
nt.pnt.example: The average spacing of primes near x has scale log x.
nt.pnt.caution: The theorem does not bound each prime gap by a fixed multiple of log x.
nt.pnt.proof_idea: An analytic proof combines nonvanishing of zeta on Re s = 1 with a Tauberian theorem.

nt.elliptic.title: Elliptic curves and rational points
nt.elliptic.define: A pointed smooth projective genus-one curve carries an arithmetic group law.
nt.elliptic.statement: An elliptic curve over K is a smooth projective geometrically integral genus-one curve with a chosen K-rational point. In characteristic different from 2 and 3 it has a model $y^2=x^3+Ax+B$, $4A^3+27B^2\ne0$.
nt.elliptic.hypotheses: The projective point at infinity is the identity in this model.
nt.elliptic.example: Chords and tangents describe the group law.
nt.elliptic.caution: A singular cubic is not an elliptic curve.

nt.mordell-weil.title: Mordell–Weil theorem
nt.mordell-weil.define: Rational points on an elliptic curve over a number field are finitely generated.
nt.mordell-weil.statement: For an elliptic curve E over a number field K, $E(K)$ is a finitely generated abelian group.
nt.mordell-weil.hypotheses: E is nonsingular and K is a number field.
nt.mordell-weil.caution: Finite generation does not mean finitely many rational points or an easy rank computation.
nt.mordell-weil.proof_idea: Finite descent classes and height reduction establish finite generation.

nt.local-global.title: Local–global principles and limits
nt.local-global.define: A nondegenerate quadratic form over a number field has a nonzero zero if and only if it has one over every completion.
nt.local-global.statement: A nondegenerate quadratic form over a number field has a nonzero zero if and only if it has one over every completion.
nt.local-global.hypotheses: The Hasse–Minkowski theorem includes every finite and Archimedean place.
nt.local-global.example: Projective conics can be tested over completions.
nt.local-global.caution: Genus-one torsors can have points over every completion but no rational point.
nt.local-global.proof_idea: Local classification of quadratic forms combines with global reciprocity; the global-to-local direction is immediate.

pr.space.title: Probability spaces and random variables
pr.space.define: Random variables are measurable maps whose laws are probability measures.
pr.space.statement: A probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ is a measure space of mass one. A random variable is a measurable map to a measurable state space; its law is the pushforward measure.
pr.space.hypotheses: Events must belong to the chosen sigma-algebra.
pr.space.example: Real random variables have laws on the Borel sets of the real line.
pr.space.caution: A random variable and its law are different objects.
pr.space.references:
PR: probability spaces.

pr.independence.title: Independence and product laws
pr.independence.define: Sigma-algebras are independent when probabilities of intersections factor for every finite subfamily. Variables are independent when their generated sigma-algebras are independent.
pr.independence.statement: Sigma-algebras are independent when probabilities of intersections factor for every finite subfamily. Variables are independent when their generated sigma-algebras are independent.
pr.independence.hypotheses: Mutual independence requires more than pairwise independence.
pr.independence.example: Two independent fair bits and their sum modulo two are pairwise independent but not mutually independent.
pr.independence.caution: Zero covariance alone does not imply independence.

pr.convergence.title: Modes of convergence
pr.convergence.define: Almost-sure, probability, distribution and mean convergence are distinct notions.
pr.convergence.statement: Almost-sure convergence implies convergence in probability, which implies convergence in distribution. $L^p$ convergence for $p\ge1$ implies convergence in probability.
pr.convergence.hypotheses: Almost-sure and probability convergence compare variables on one probability space; convergence in law compares distributions.
pr.convergence.example: Rare tall spikes may converge in probability without converging in mean.
pr.convergence.caution: Convergence in law generally does not imply convergence in probability.

pr.borel-cantelli.title: Borel–Cantelli lemmas
pr.borel-cantelli.define: Summable event probabilities prevent infinitely many occurrences almost surely.
pr.borel-cantelli.statement: If $\sum_n\mathbb P(A_n)<\infty$, only finitely many $A_n$ occur almost surely. If the events are independent and the sum diverges, infinitely many occur almost surely.
pr.borel-cantelli.hypotheses: Independence is needed for the second conclusion in this version.
pr.borel-cantelli.example: Independent fair tosses produce infinitely many heads almost surely.
pr.borel-cantelli.caution: Divergence of the sum for dependent events does not suffice.
pr.borel-cantelli.proof_idea: A union bound proves the first part; independence and a product bound prove the second.

pr.slln.title: Strong law of large numbers
pr.slln.define: Independent identically distributed integrable averages converge almost surely to the mean.
pr.slln.statement: For iid real variables with $\mathbb E|X_1|<\infty$, $n^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^nX_k\to\mathbb E X_1$ almost surely.
pr.slln.hypotheses: The variables are independent, identically distributed and absolutely integrable.
pr.slln.example: Empirical event frequencies converge to their probabilities.
pr.slln.caution: Finite variance is unnecessary, but an undefined mean cannot appear as the limit here.
pr.slln.proof_idea: Truncate large values, control centered partial sums, apply Borel–Cantelli and remove truncation.

pr.characteristic.title: Characteristic functions
pr.characteristic.define: Fourier transforms of probability laws encode distributions and independent sums.
pr.characteristic.statement: The function $\varphi_X(t)=\mathbb E e^{itX}$ determines the law of a real variable. Independence turns characteristic functions of sums into products.
pr.characteristic.hypotheses: The bounded exponential ensures existence for every real random variable.
pr.characteristic.caution: Moment-generating functions, unlike characteristic functions, need not exist near zero.

pr.weak.title: Weak convergence and Portmanteau
pr.weak.define: Weak convergence is tested by bounded continuous functions and closed-set inequalities.
pr.weak.statement: For Borel probability measures on a metric space, weak convergence means convergence of integrals of all bounded continuous real functions. Equivalently, $\limsup_n\mu_n(F)\le\mu(F)$ for every closed F.
pr.weak.hypotheses: The measures live on the same metric space.
pr.weak.example: Probabilities converge for sets whose boundary has limiting measure zero.
pr.weak.caution: Integrals of unbounded continuous functions need not converge.
pr.weak.proof_idea: Approximate closed-set indicators by distance cutoffs and use level-set bounds for the converse.

pr.clt.title: Central limit theorem
pr.clt.define: Finite-variance independent identically distributed sums have a Gaussian scaling limit.
pr.clt.statement: For iid real variables with mean $\mu$ and variance $0<\sigma^2<\infty$, $(\sum_{k=1}^nX_k-n\mu)/(\sigma\sqrt n)$ converges in law to $N(0,1)$.
pr.clt.hypotheses: This version assumes finite, strictly positive variance.
pr.clt.example: Standardized binomial counts approach the normal law.
pr.clt.caution: Infinite-variance laws may require different scaling and different limits.
pr.clt.proof_idea: Expand the characteristic function at zero to second order and apply its continuity theorem.
pr.clt.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

pr.conditional.title: Conditional expectation
pr.conditional.define: Conditional expectation matches integrals on all events observable in a sub-sigma-algebra.
pr.conditional.statement: For $X\in L^1$ and a sub-sigma-algebra $\mathcal G$, there is a $\mathcal G$-measurable integrable Y such that $\int_A Y\,d\mathbb P=\int_A X\,d\mathbb P$ for all $A\in\mathcal G$. It is unique almost surely and denoted $\mathbb E[X\mid\mathcal G]$.
pr.conditional.hypotheses: Equality and uniqueness are modulo null sets.
pr.conditional.example: For a finite partition, conditioning averages over cells of positive probability.
pr.conditional.caution: The elementary ratio formula cannot condition directly on a probability-zero event.
pr.conditional.proof_idea: Apply Radon–Nikodym to positive and negative parts on the sub-sigma-algebra.

pr.regular.title: Regular conditional distributions
pr.regular.define: For random elements X,Y in standard Borel spaces, the conditional law of X given Y admits a probability-kernel version K(y,A) satisfying the conditional integral identities.
pr.regular.statement: For random elements X,Y in standard Borel spaces, the conditional law of X given Y admits a probability-kernel version K(y,A) satisfying the conditional integral identities.
pr.regular.hypotheses: A standard Borel space is measurably isomorphic to a Borel subset of a Polish space.
pr.regular.example: Conditional densities, when available, give concrete kernels.
pr.regular.caution: Versions can differ on Y-null sets; arbitrary measurable spaces need not admit such kernels.
pr.regular.proof_idea: Construct conditional probabilities on a countable determining family and extend to measures.

pr.ui.title: Uniform integrability
pr.ui.define: Uniform tail control is the missing ingredient for convergence in mean.
pr.ui.statement: A family $\mathcal X\subset L^1$ is uniformly integrable if $\sup_{X\in\mathcal X}\mathbb E[|X|1_{|X|>K}]\to0$. For integrable X, convergence in probability plus uniform integrability of the sequence is equivalent to $L^1$ convergence.
pr.ui.hypotheses: All variables are on one probability space.
pr.ui.example: A uniform Lp bound for some p greater than one implies uniform integrability.
pr.ui.caution: Uniform L1 boundedness alone allows rare tall spikes and is insufficient.
pr.ui.prerequisites:

pr.martingale.title: Filtrations and martingales
pr.martingale.define: A martingale preserves its conditional mean as information grows.
pr.martingale.statement: A filtration is an increasing sequence $\mathcal F_n$ of sigma-algebras. An integrable adapted process is a martingale if $\mathbb E[M_{n+1}\mid\mathcal F_n]=M_n$ almost surely.
pr.martingale.hypotheses: The filtration is part of the data.
pr.martingale.example: Centered partial sums of independent integrable increments form a martingale.
pr.martingale.caution: Martingales need not have independent increments.
pr.martingale.references:
PR: martingales.

pr.doob.title: Doob maximal inequality
pr.doob.define: A terminal Lp bound controls the maximum along a finite martingale path.
pr.doob.statement: For a discrete-time martingale, finite horizon n and $p>1$, $\|\max_{0\le k\le n}|M_k|\|_p\le p/(p-1)\,\|M_n\|_p$.
pr.doob.hypotheses: The terminal value is in Lp.
pr.doob.example: The terminal Lp size controls the maximum along a finite path.
pr.doob.caution: The strong inequality has no finite constant of this form at p = 1.
pr.doob.proof_idea: Stop at the first threshold crossing, bound the tail and integrate using Holder's inequality.

pr.stopping.title: Optional stopping
pr.stopping.define: Optional stopping preserves martingale identities under boundedness or uniform integrability.
pr.stopping.statement: For a discrete-time martingale and bounded stopping times $S\le T$, $\mathbb E[M_T\mid\mathcal F_S]=M_S$. The same holds for almost-surely finite S,T when the martingale is uniformly integrable.
pr.stopping.hypotheses: Stopping times cannot depend on future information; integrability controls passage to limits.
pr.stopping.example: Stopping an integrable fair game before a fixed round preserves expected capital.
pr.stopping.caution: An unbounded doubling strategy lacks the required integrability control.
pr.stopping.proof_idea: Sum stopped increments at finite horizons, then use uniform integrability for unbounded horizons.
pr.stopping.references:
PR: optional stopping.

pr.martingale-limit.title: Martingale convergence
pr.martingale-limit.define: L1-bounded martingales converge almost surely; uniform integrability strengthens the limit.
pr.martingale-limit.statement: If $\sup_n\mathbb E|M_n|<\infty$, a discrete-time martingale converges almost surely to an integrable limit. Under uniform integrability it also converges in $L^1$ and $M_n=\mathbb E[M_\infty\mid\mathcal F_n]$.
pr.martingale-limit.hypotheses: L1 boundedness and uniform integrability have distinct consequences.
pr.martingale-limit.example: Nonnegative martingales converge almost surely but can lose expectation in the limit.
pr.martingale-limit.caution: L1 boundedness alone does not ensure L1 convergence.
pr.martingale-limit.proof_idea: The upcrossing inequality excludes oscillation; Fatou gives integrability and uniform integrability justifies the conditional limit.
pr.martingale-limit.references:
PR: martingale convergence.

pr.markov.title: Finite-state Markov chains
pr.markov.define: An irreducible finite-state Markov chain has a unique stationary probability vector. If also aperiodic, its distribution converges to that vector from every initial distribution.
pr.markov.statement: An irreducible finite-state Markov chain has a unique stationary probability vector. If also aperiodic, its distribution converges to that vector from every initial distribution.
pr.markov.hypotheses: Transition-matrix rows sum to one; irreducibility means all states communicate.
pr.markov.example: Deterministic alternation between two states is irreducible but periodic.
pr.markov.caution: Stationarity alone does not guarantee convergence.
pr.markov.proof_idea: Irreducibility yields the stationary eigenvector; aperiodicity removes other peripheral eigenvalues.
pr.markov.references:

pr.extension.title: Kolmogorov extension theorem
pr.extension.define: A consistent family of finite-dimensional probability laws on products of standard Borel state spaces determines a unique probability measure on the cylinder sigma-algebra of the full product.
pr.extension.statement: A consistent family of finite-dimensional probability laws on products of standard Borel state spaces determines a unique probability measure on the cylinder sigma-algebra of the full product.
pr.extension.hypotheses: Marginalization and coordinate permutations preserve the prescribed laws.
pr.extension.example: Consistent Gaussian laws of covariance min(s,t) specify Brownian finite-dimensional distributions.
pr.extension.caution: Extension alone does not give continuous sample paths.
pr.extension.proof_idea: Define cylinder probabilities and use the state-space regularity to establish the countable additivity needed for extension.

pr.brownian.title: Brownian motion
pr.brownian.define: Brownian motion has continuous paths and independent Gaussian increments.
pr.brownian.statement: Standard Brownian motion starts at zero, has continuous paths and independent stationary increments with $B_t-B_s\sim N(0,t-s)$ for $0\le s<t$.
pr.brownian.hypotheses: For stochastic calculus the filtration must make future increments independent of present information.
pr.brownian.caution: Paths are almost surely nowhere differentiable despite continuity.

pr.ito-integral.title: Itô integral and isometry
pr.ito-integral.define: The Brownian stochastic integral is constructed by an L2 isometry.
pr.ito-integral.statement: For predictable H with $\mathbb E\int_0^T H_t^2dt<\infty$, the Brownian integral obeys $\mathbb E(\int_0^T H_t\,dB_t)^2=\mathbb E\int_0^T H_t^2dt$.
pr.ito-integral.hypotheses: Use a Brownian filtration with the usual conditions and square integrability in time and probability.
pr.ito-integral.caution: This is not ordinary integration against a path of bounded variation.
pr.ito-integral.proof_idea: Define the integral on adapted step processes, prove the isometry by independent increments and complete in L2.

pr.ito-formula.title: Itô's formula
pr.ito-formula.define: The stochastic chain rule includes a second-order quadratic-variation correction.
pr.ito-formula.statement: For $f\in C^{1,2}([0,T]\times\mathbb R)$, $df(t,B_t)=(f_t+\tfrac12f_{xx})(t,B_t)dt+f_x(t,B_t)dB_t$, locally when global integrability is unavailable.
pr.ito-formula.hypotheses: One continuous time derivative and two continuous spatial derivatives suffice in this version.
pr.ito-formula.caution: The second-derivative term records quadratic variation and cannot be omitted.
pr.ito-formula.proof_idea: Taylor-expand along partitions; squared increments converge to elapsed time and higher-order remainders vanish after localization.

sl.sets.title: Sets, functions and relations
sl.sets.define: Sets collect elements; a binary relation is a subset of a Cartesian product. A function is a relation assigning exactly one output to each input in its domain.
sl.sets.statement: Sets collect elements; a binary relation is a subset of a Cartesian product. A function is a relation assigning exactly one output to each input in its domain.
sl.sets.hypotheses: Collections too large to be sets are handled as classes in the metatheory or in a class theory.
sl.sets.example: An equivalence relation partitions a set; its quotient consists of equivalence classes.
sl.sets.caution: Unrestricted comprehension is inconsistent: the Russell collection cannot be a set.
sl.sets.prerequisites: Entry point; see the subject guide for assumed background.

sl.syntax.title: First-order syntax and proofs
sl.syntax.define: A first-order language specifies function, relation and constant symbols with arities. Terms and formulas are finite strings built recursively; formal proofs use fixed effective inference rules.
sl.syntax.statement: A first-order language specifies function, relation and constant symbols with arities. Terms and formulas are finite strings built recursively; formal proofs use fixed effective inference rules.
sl.syntax.hypotheses: Quantifiers range over individuals, not over all subsets or relations.
sl.syntax.example: In the language of groups, associativity is a first-order sentence.
sl.syntax.caution: A formula with free variables differs from a sentence; bound-variable renaming must avoid capture.

LOGIC: first-order languages.

sl.semantics.title: Structures, satisfaction and elementary maps
sl.semantics.define: Structures interpret syntax; elementary maps preserve all first-order formulas.
sl.semantics.statement: A structure interprets the symbols on a nonempty domain. Satisfaction $\mathcal M\models\varphi[\bar a]$ is defined recursively. An elementary embedding preserves every first-order formula with parameters.
sl.semantics.hypotheses: Classical first-order semantics and nonempty domains are used.
sl.semantics.example: The inclusion of one group in another preserves operations but need not be elementary.
sl.semantics.caution: Truth in one structure is different from validity in all structures.
sl.semantics.references:
LOGIC: structures and satisfaction.

sl.soundness.title: Soundness
sl.soundness.define: Formal derivability implies semantic consequence for a sound proof calculus.
sl.soundness.statement: For a standard classical first-order proof calculus, $T\vdash\varphi$ implies $T\models\varphi$.
sl.soundness.hypotheses: Proof rules must be sound for the specified semantics, including the variable restrictions on quantifier rules.
sl.soundness.example: No false conclusion can follow by these rules from premises true in a structure.
sl.soundness.caution: Soundness does not assert that T's nonlogical axioms are true in an intended structure.
sl.soundness.proof_idea: Induct on proof length, checking that each rule preserves truth under assignments.

sl.completeness.title: Gödel completeness theorem
sl.completeness.define: Every first-order semantic consequence has a finite formal proof.
sl.completeness.statement: For classical first-order logic, $T\models\varphi$ implies $T\vdash\varphi$. Equivalently, every syntactically consistent first-order theory has a model.
sl.completeness.hypotheses: The ambient metatheory supplies ordinary classical set-theoretic reasoning.
sl.completeness.example: Semantic impossibility of a first-order configuration yields a finite formal refutation.
sl.completeness.caution: Completeness of logic does not mean that each particular theory decides every sentence.
sl.completeness.proof_idea: Add Henkin witnesses, extend to a maximally consistent theory and build its term model.
sl.completeness.references:
LOGIC: completeness.

- **LOGIC** — Open Logic Project contributors. [Open Logic Text](https://builds.openlogicproject.org/open-logic-complete.pdf). Living open textbook; first-order logic, computability and set theory.

sl.compactness.title: Compactness theorem
sl.compactness.define: A first-order theory has a model if every finite subset has a model.
sl.compactness.statement: A first-order theory has a model if every finite subset has a model.
sl.compactness.hypotheses: This concerns finitary first-order logic, with ordinary classical semantics.
sl.compactness.example: Adding a constant larger than every standard numeral produces a nonstandard model of arithmetic by compactness.
sl.compactness.caution: Compactness fails for full second-order semantics.
sl.compactness.proof_idea: A formal contradiction uses only finitely many axioms; completeness supplies the model.
sl.compactness.references:
LOGIC: compactness.

sl.lowenheim-skolem.title: Downward Löwenheim–Skolem theorem
sl.lowenheim-skolem.define: Infinite structures have small elementary substructures containing specified parameters.
sl.lowenheim-skolem.statement: For an infinite structure M in language L and $A\subseteq M$, there is an elementary substructure containing A of cardinality at most $\max(|A|,|L|,\aleph_0)$.
sl.lowenheim-skolem.hypotheses: The theorem is stated in ordinary ZFC metatheory.
sl.lowenheim-skolem.example: A countable-language theory with an infinite model has a countable model.
sl.lowenheim-skolem.caution: An externally countable model may internally regard some of its sets as uncountable; its internal bijections are restricted.
sl.lowenheim-skolem.proof_idea: Close the parameter set under chosen witnesses for existential formulas and apply the Tarski–Vaught criterion.

sl.computability.title: Computability and enumerable theories
sl.computability.define: A set is decidable if a Turing machine always halts and correctly decides membership. It is computably enumerable if a machine enumerates its members, equivalently semidecides membership.
sl.computability.statement: A set is decidable if a Turing machine always halts and correctly decides membership. It is computably enumerable if a machine enumerates its members, equivalently semidecides membership.
sl.computability.hypotheses: Fix an effective coding of finite strings, machines and proofs.
sl.computability.example: The theorems of an effectively axiomatized theory are computably enumerable.
sl.computability.caution: Enumerable need not mean decidable; failure of a search to halt is not a negative answer.
sl.computability.references:
LOGIC: Turing machines and computability.

sl.halting.title: Undecidability of halting
sl.halting.define: No algorithm decides, for every encoded machine and input, whether that computation eventually halts.
sl.halting.statement: No algorithm decides, for every encoded machine and input, whether that computation eventually halts.
sl.halting.hypotheses: The input describes arbitrary computations in a universal effective model.
sl.halting.example: The halting set is computably enumerable but not decidable.
sl.halting.caution: Undecidability of the general problem does not prevent deciding many particular programs.
sl.halting.proof_idea: A hypothetical decider yields a program that halts on its own code exactly when the decider predicts nonhalting.
sl.halting.references:
LOGIC: halting problem.

sl.incompleteness-one.title: First incompleteness theorem
sl.incompleteness-one.define: Every consistent computably axiomatizable theory extending Robinson arithmetic Q is incomplete: some sentence is neither provable nor refutable in the theory.
sl.incompleteness-one.statement: Every consistent computably axiomatizable theory extending Robinson arithmetic Q is incomplete: some sentence is neither provable nor refutable in the theory.
sl.incompleteness-one.hypotheses: This is the Gödel–Rosser formulation; consistency, effective axiomatization and sufficient arithmetic are essential.
sl.incompleteness-one.example: If PA is consistent, it does not decide all arithmetic sentences.
sl.incompleteness-one.caution: Complete theories exist, but true arithmetic is not computably axiomatizable; logical completeness is a different statement.
sl.incompleteness-one.proof_idea: Encode syntax arithmetically and diagonalize; Rosser's refinement needs consistency rather than omega-consistency.

sl.incompleteness-two.title: Second incompleteness theorem
sl.incompleteness-two.define: Consistent effective extensions of PA cannot prove their standard consistency sentence.
sl.incompleteness-two.statement: A consistent computably axiomatized extension T of PA cannot prove its standard arithmetical consistency sentence $\operatorname{Con}(T)$.
sl.incompleteness-two.hypotheses: Use the usual arithmetized proof predicate satisfying the derivability conditions.
sl.incompleteness-two.example: A stronger theory may prove the consistency of a weaker one without contradiction.
sl.incompleteness-two.caution: The theorem is sensitive to the consistency formalization and is not a blanket ban on all metamathematical consistency proofs.
sl.incompleteness-two.proof_idea: Formalize the diagonal argument inside arithmetic and show that a proof of consistency would yield the unprovable diagonal sentence.

sl.zf.title: ZF axioms and the cumulative hierarchy
sl.zf.define: ZF organizes sets by explicit axioms and the cumulative hierarchy.
sl.zf.statement: ZF consists of extensionality, empty set, pairing, union, power set, infinity, separation and replacement schemes, and foundation. The hierarchy has $V_0=\varnothing$, $V_{\alpha+1}=\mathcal P(V_\alpha)$ and unions at limit stages.
sl.zf.hypotheses: ZF does not include the axiom of choice; the schemes contain infinitely many first-order instances.
sl.zf.example: Separation selects a subset of an already given set.
sl.zf.caution: The cumulative hierarchy is a proper class, not a set containing all sets.

sl.ordinals.title: Ordinals and well-orders
sl.ordinals.define: An ordinal is a transitive set well-ordered by membership. Each well-ordered set is order-isomorphic to a unique ordinal.
sl.ordinals.statement: An ordinal is a transitive set well-ordered by membership. Each well-ordered set is order-isomorphic to a unique ordinal.
sl.ordinals.hypotheses: This uses the standard von Neumann representation.
sl.ordinals.example: $\omega+1$ and $1+\omega=\omega$ show that ordinal addition is not commutative.
sl.ordinals.caution: Order type and cardinal size are different invariants.
sl.ordinals.references:
LOGIC: ordinals.

sl.transfinite.title: Transfinite induction and recursion
sl.transfinite.define: For a well-ordered domain, induction from all earlier stages proves a property at every stage. A functional rule assigning a set from each prior segment defines a unique recursively constructed sequence along any ordinal.
sl.transfinite.statement: For a well-ordered domain, induction from all earlier stages proves a property at every stage. A functional rule assigning a set from each prior segment defines a unique recursively constructed sequence along any ordinal.
sl.transfinite.hypotheses: The recursive rule must be functional; replacement collects the values into sets at set-sized stages.
sl.transfinite.example: The cumulative hierarchy and ordinal arithmetic are defined recursively.
sl.transfinite.caution: At limit stages one must specify the rule; there is no immediate predecessor.
sl.transfinite.proof_idea: A least counterexample proves induction; compatible partial solutions are glued by uniqueness and extended at each stage.
sl.transfinite.references:
LOGIC: transfinite recursion.

sl.cardinals.title: Cardinals and countability
sl.cardinals.define: Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. In ZFC each cardinal has a least ordinal representative, and any two cardinalities are comparable.
sl.cardinals.statement: Two sets have the same cardinality if there is a bijection between them. In ZFC each cardinal has a least ordinal representative, and any two cardinalities are comparable.
sl.cardinals.hypotheses: Well-orderability of every set uses choice.
sl.cardinals.example: The integers and rationals are countable; the real numbers are not.
sl.cardinals.caution: An infinite subset can have the same cardinality as its proper superset.

sl.cantor.title: Cantor's theorem
sl.cantor.define: No set can be mapped onto its entire power set.
sl.cantor.statement: For every set A there is no surjection $A\to\mathcal P(A)$; thus A has strictly smaller cardinality than its power set.
sl.cantor.hypotheses: The diagonal argument requires no axiom of choice.
sl.cantor.caution: There is no largest cardinal and no set of all sets.
sl.cantor.proof_idea: For a proposed surjection f, the set of a not belonging to f(a) differs from every image value.
sl.cantor.references:
LOGIC: Cantor theorem.

sl.choice.title: Axiom of choice, Zorn and well-ordering
sl.choice.define: Over ZF, the axiom of choice, the well-ordering theorem and Zorn's lemma are equivalent. Zorn's lemma says that a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound has a maximal element.
sl.choice.statement: Over ZF, the axiom of choice, the well-ordering theorem and Zorn's lemma are equivalent. Zorn's lemma says that a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound has a maximal element.
sl.choice.hypotheses: A maximal element need not be a greatest element.
sl.choice.example: Zorn's lemma yields a basis for every vector space.
sl.choice.caution: Countable and dependent choice are weaker principles and should not be silently identified with full choice.
sl.choice.proof_idea: Choice builds maximal chains by transfinite methods; suitable partial choice functions recover choice from Zorn.

sl.ch.title: Continuum hypothesis and independence
sl.ch.define: The continuum hypothesis is independent of ZFC, assuming ZFC is consistent.
sl.ch.statement: CH asserts $2^{\aleph_0}=\aleph_1$. If ZFC is consistent, both ZFC + CH and ZFC + not-CH are consistent. Consequently ZFC proves neither CH nor its negation under that consistency assumption.
sl.ch.hypotheses: This is relative consistency, not a proof that ZFC is consistent.
sl.ch.example: The constructible universe supplies CH; forcing supplies models where CH fails.
sl.ch.caution: Independence is always relative to a specified axiom system.
sl.ch.proof_idea: Gödel's constructible universe gives one direction; Cohen forcing gives the other via a metatheoretic consistency argument.

sl.forcing.title: Forcing and generic extensions
sl.forcing.define: Generic extensions modify a model's sets while preserving its ordinals and ZFC.
sl.forcing.statement: For a countable transitive model M of ZFC and a forcing notion $\mathbb P\in M$, an externally chosen M-generic filter yields an extension M[G] satisfying ZFC, with the same ordinals.
sl.forcing.hypotheses: This introductory semantic setup assumes a countable transitive model; its existence is stronger than merely Con(ZFC). Conditions may be ordered with stronger conditions below weaker ones.
sl.forcing.example: Cohen forcing adds a new subset of the natural numbers.
sl.forcing.caution: A generic filter is generally outside M. Full relative-consistency proofs need not assume that a transitive model actually exists.

sl.types.title: Types and saturation
sl.types.define: A type over parameters is a consistent collection of formulas in fixed free variables. A saturated model realizes types over parameter sets smaller than its saturation cardinal.
sl.types.statement: A type over parameters is a consistent collection of formulas in fixed free variables. A saturated model realizes types over parameter sets smaller than its saturation cardinal.
sl.types.hypotheses: Specify the theory, the parameter set and the saturation cardinal.
sl.types.example: The type saying a number exceeds each standard numeral is realized in a suitable nonstandard model.
sl.types.caution: Compactness can realize a type in an extension without making a given model saturated.

tp.spaces.title: Topological spaces and continuity
tp.spaces.define: A topology contains the empty set and the whole space, is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A map is continuous when inverse images of open sets are open.
tp.spaces.statement: A topology contains the empty set and the whole space, is closed under arbitrary unions and finite intersections. A map is continuous when inverse images of open sets are open.
tp.spaces.hypotheses: Open sets, rather than a chosen metric, are the primitive data.
tp.spaces.example: The discrete and indiscrete topologies put very different structures on the same underlying set.
tp.spaces.caution: Sequential continuity need not characterize continuity in arbitrary spaces.

tp.metric.title: Metric and Polish spaces
tp.metric.define: A metric induces open balls and hence a topology. A Polish space is separable and completely metrizable: some compatible metric is complete.
tp.metric.statement: A metric induces open balls and hence a topology. A Polish space is separable and completely metrizable: some compatible metric is complete.
tp.metric.hypotheses: Completeness depends on the metric; complete metrizability is a property of the topology.
tp.metric.example: An open interval is Polish although its usual Euclidean metric is not complete.
tp.metric.caution: Not every topological space is metrizable.

tp.subspace.title: Subspace, product and quotient topologies
tp.subspace.define: Subspaces inherit intersections with ambient open sets. Product topology is generated by finite-coordinate restrictions. A quotient map declares a set open exactly when its preimage is open.
tp.subspace.statement: Subspaces inherit intersections with ambient open sets. Product topology is generated by finite-coordinate restrictions. A quotient map declares a set open exactly when its preimage is open.
tp.subspace.hypotheses: The infinite product topology differs from the box topology.
tp.subspace.example: Identifying the endpoints of a closed interval produces a circle.
tp.subspace.caution: Quotients of Hausdorff spaces need not be Hausdorff.

tp.separation.title: Separation axioms
tp.separation.define: A Hausdorff space separates distinct points by disjoint open neighborhoods. A regular T1 space separates a point from a disjoint closed set; a normal T1 space separates disjoint closed sets.
tp.separation.statement: A Hausdorff space separates distinct points by disjoint open neighborhoods. A regular T1 space separates a point from a disjoint closed set; a normal T1 space separates disjoint closed sets.
tp.separation.hypotheses: The T1 condition is included explicitly in the regular and normal conventions here.
tp.separation.example: Metric spaces are normal and Hausdorff.
tp.separation.caution: Separation axioms are distinct from countability axioms.
tp.separation.references:
TOP: separation properties.

tp.compact.title: Compactness and Hausdorff spaces
tp.compact.define: A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover. A continuous image of a compact space is compact; compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed.
tp.compact.statement: A space is compact when every open cover has a finite subcover. A continuous image of a compact space is compact; compact subsets of Hausdorff spaces are closed.
tp.compact.hypotheses: Hausdorffness is needed for the closedness conclusion.
tp.compact.example: Closed bounded subsets of Euclidean space are compact.
tp.compact.caution: Closed bounded subsets of infinite-dimensional normed spaces need not be compact.
tp.compact.proof_idea: Pull covers back along the map; use Hausdorff neighborhoods and a finite subcover to separate points from compact sets.

tp.tychonoff.title: Tychonoff theorem
tp.tychonoff.define: An arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.
tp.tychonoff.statement: An arbitrary product of compact spaces is compact in the product topology.
tp.tychonoff.hypotheses: This form is stated in ZFC; the corresponding general theorem is equivalent to choice over ZF.
tp.tychonoff.example: Products of closed bounded intervals are compact, including products with infinitely many factors.
tp.tychonoff.caution: Using the box topology instead invalidates the general conclusion.
tp.tychonoff.proof_idea: Extend a family with the finite-intersection property to an ultrafilter and use convergence in every coordinate.

tp.connected.title: Connectedness and path connectedness
tp.connected.define: A connected space has no decomposition into two disjoint nonempty open subsets. A path-connected space joins every two points by a continuous map from the unit interval.
tp.connected.statement: A connected space has no decomposition into two disjoint nonempty open subsets. A path-connected space joins every two points by a continuous map from the unit interval.
tp.connected.hypotheses: Path connectedness implies connectedness; the converse requires further hypotheses.
tp.connected.example: The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path connected.
tp.connected.caution: Local connectedness and global connectedness are different properties.
tp.connected.references:
TOP: connectedness.

tp.metrization.title: Urysohn metrization theorem
tp.metrization.define: Every second-countable regular T1 space is metrizable.
tp.metrization.statement: Every second-countable regular T1 space is metrizable.
tp.metrization.hypotheses: Second countability means a countable base, not merely a countable dense subset.
tp.metrization.example: The theorem supplies compatible metrics for many abstractly defined spaces.
tp.metrization.caution: A general regular separable space need not be metrizable.
tp.metrization.proof_idea: Construct countably many continuous functions separating points and embed the space in a countable cube.

tp.homotopy.title: Homotopies and homotopy equivalence
tp.homotopy.define: Homotopies deform maps continuously; homotopy equivalences preserve algebraic invariants.
tp.homotopy.statement: Maps f,g are homotopic when a continuous $H:X\times[0,1]\to Y$ interpolates between them. A homotopy equivalence has an inverse up to homotopy.
tp.homotopy.hypotheses: For based constructions, specify which basepoints are fixed throughout.
tp.homotopy.example: A punctured plane deformation retracts onto a circle.
tp.homotopy.caution: Homotopy equivalence is weaker than homeomorphism.

tp.fundamental.title: Fundamental group
tp.fundamental.define: Based loops modulo homotopy form a group detecting one-dimensional holes.
tp.fundamental.statement: The group $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ consists of based loops modulo based homotopy, with concatenation as multiplication. Continuous based maps induce homomorphisms.
tp.fundamental.hypotheses: In a path-connected space basepoint changes give isomorphisms, generally dependent on a chosen path.
tp.fundamental.caution: The fundamental group alone does not determine the homotopy type.
tp.fundamental.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Homotopies and homotopy equivalence](./notes/tp.homotopy.md)

**From other subjects**

tp.van-kampen.title: Seifert–van Kampen theorem
tp.van-kampen.define: Compatible open decompositions compute fundamental groups by a group pushout.
tp.van-kampen.statement: If $X=U\cup V$ with U,V and their intersection path connected and U,V open, $\pi_1(X)$ is the pushout of $\pi_1(U)$ and $\pi_1(V)$ over $\pi_1(U\cap V)$.
tp.van-kampen.hypotheses: Choose the basepoint in the intersection; disconnected intersections require a more general formulation.
tp.van-kampen.example: A bouquet of two circles has free fundamental group on two generators.
tp.van-kampen.caution: An arbitrary closed cover does not meet these stated hypotheses.
tp.van-kampen.proof_idea: Subdivide loops and homotopies along the cover, then identify exactly the intersection relations.

tp.coverings.title: Covering-space classification
tp.coverings.define: Under local connectivity assumptions, connected coverings correspond to subgroups.
tp.coverings.statement: For connected, locally path-connected, semilocally simply connected X, connected based coverings correspond to subgroups of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$. Unbased coverings correspond to conjugacy classes of subgroups.
tp.coverings.hypotheses: A covering is locally a disjoint union of homeomorphic sheets.
tp.coverings.example: $z\mapsto z^n$ gives an n-sheeted cover of the circle.
tp.coverings.caution: Dropping the local assumptions can break this classification and existence of a universal cover.
tp.coverings.proof_idea: Path lifting gives the subgroup; homotopy classes of paths construct the covering with a prescribed subgroup.
tp.coverings.prerequisites:

tp.manifolds.title: Topological manifolds
tp.manifolds.define: Topological manifolds are locally Euclidean spaces with separation and countability conditions.
tp.manifolds.statement: An n-manifold is a Hausdorff second-countable space locally homeomorphic to $\mathbb R^n$. Manifolds with boundary instead use a closed half-space in their local models.
tp.manifolds.hypotheses: The boundary convention must be specified; a manifold here has no boundary unless stated.
tp.manifolds.example: Spheres and tori are compact manifolds.
tp.manifolds.caution: A topological manifold is not automatically supplied with a smooth structure.
tp.manifolds.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Separation axioms](./notes/tp.separation.md)

tp.cw.title: CW complexes
tp.cw.define: A CW complex is built inductively by attaching disks along their boundary spheres, with the closure-finite and weak-topology conditions.
tp.cw.statement: A CW complex is built inductively by attaching disks along their boundary spheres, with the closure-finite and weak-topology conditions.
tp.cw.hypotheses: Attaching maps need not be embeddings.
tp.cw.example: A circle has one 0-cell and one 1-cell; a torus has a standard finite cell structure.
tp.cw.caution: A cell decomposition is extra structure and is not unique.
tp.cw.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

tp.homology.title: Singular homology
tp.homology.define: Homology records cycles modulo boundaries in a chain complex.
tp.homology.statement: Singular chains are finite linear combinations of maps from simplices to X. The alternating face boundary satisfies $\partial^2=0$, giving $H_n(X;R)=\ker\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\partial_{n+1}$.
tp.homology.hypotheses: Fix a coefficient ring; homology is functorial and homotopy invariant.
tp.homology.caution: Cycles need not be boundaries; the quotient records precisely this difference.
tp.homology.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Homotopies and homotopy equivalence](./notes/tp.homotopy.md)

**From other subjects**

- [Normal subgroups and quotients](./notes/gt.quotients.md) — Group theory

tp.exact.title: Long exact sequence of a pair
tp.exact.define: Relative homology connects a subspace, its ambient space and their pair.
tp.exact.statement: For $A\subseteq X$, relative chains give $\cdots\to H_n(A)\to H_n(X)\to H_n(X,A)\to H_{n-1}(A)\to\cdots$.
tp.exact.hypotheses: All groups use the same coefficients; relative chains are the quotient chain complex.
tp.exact.example: The pair consisting of a disk and its boundary computes sphere homology.
tp.exact.caution: Exactness means image equals kernel, not that all maps are injective or surjective.
tp.exact.proof_idea: Lift a relative cycle, take its boundary in A and check the resulting connecting map and exactness.
tp.exact.references:
AT: relative homology.

- **AT** — Allen Hatcher. [Algebraic Topology](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html). Cambridge University Press, 2002; author-hosted text.

tp.excision.title: Excision
tp.excision.define: Removing a suitably interior subset preserves relative homology.
tp.excision.statement: If $U\subseteq A\subseteq X$ and $\overline U\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X A$, inclusion induces $H_n(X\setminus U,A\setminus U)\cong H_n(X,A)$ for every n.
tp.excision.hypotheses: The closure-interior condition is taken in X.
tp.excision.example: Excision turns suitable local relative-homology calculations into computations in a small neighborhood.
tp.excision.caution: Removing an arbitrary subset from both members of a pair need not preserve relative homology.
tp.excision.proof_idea: Repeated barycentric subdivision makes chains small enough for the relevant open cover.
tp.excision.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Long exact sequence of a pair](./notes/tp.exact.md)
tp.excision.references:
AT: excision.

tp.mayer-vietoris.title: Mayer–Vietoris sequence
tp.mayer-vietoris.define: An open cover relates homology of the pieces, their intersection and their union.
tp.mayer-vietoris.statement: For an open cover $X=U\cup V$, homology fits into $\cdots\to H_n(U\cap V)\to H_n(U)\oplus H_n(V)\to H_n(X)\to H_{n-1}(U\cap V)\to\cdots$.
tp.mayer-vietoris.hypotheses: Use a consistent sign convention for the two inclusion maps.
tp.mayer-vietoris.example: Two enlarged hemispheres compute the reduced homology of a sphere.
tp.mayer-vietoris.caution: The intersection carries gluing information and cannot generally be discarded.
tp.mayer-vietoris.proof_idea: Use small chains for the cover and the short exact sequence comparing intersection, pieces and union.
tp.mayer-vietoris.references:
AT: Mayer-Vietoris.

- **AT** — Allen Hatcher. [Algebraic Topology](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html). Cambridge University Press, 2002; author-hosted text.

tp.cohomology.title: Cohomology and cup product
tp.cohomology.define: Cohomology adds a graded product to the additive invariants of a space.
tp.cohomology.statement: Applying $\operatorname{Hom}(-,R)$ to chains gives cohomology $H^*(X;R)$. The cup product makes it a graded ring with $ab=(-1)^{pq}ba$ for degrees p,q and commutative coefficients.
tp.cohomology.hypotheses: Integral cohomology is not always just the dual of integral homology; Ext terms can appear.
tp.cohomology.example: The cup product distinguishes spaces with identical additive cohomology groups.
tp.cohomology.caution: Chain-level cup products need not be strictly graded commutative before passing to cohomology.
tp.cohomology.references:
AT: cohomology and cup products.

- **AT** — Allen Hatcher. [Algebraic Topology](https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/ATpage.html). Cambridge University Press, 2002; author-hosted text.

tp.poincare.title: Poincaré duality
tp.poincare.define: Orientation pairs complementary homology and cohomology degrees on a closed manifold.
tp.poincare.statement: For a closed connected oriented n-manifold M, cap product with its fundamental class gives $H^k(M;\mathbb Z)\cong H_{n-k}(M;\mathbb Z)$.
tp.poincare.hypotheses: Closed means compact without boundary; nonorientable manifolds require suitable coefficients or local systems.
tp.poincare.example: On an oriented closed surface, first cohomology pairs nondegenerately by intersection.
tp.poincare.caution: For noncompact manifolds or manifolds with boundary the duality statement needs compact supports or relative groups.
tp.poincare.proof_idea: Patch local orientation classes using relative homology and Mayer–Vietoris.
tp.poincare.prerequisites:

- [Cohomology and cup product](./notes/tp.cohomology.md)

AT: Poincare duality.

dg.smooth.title: Smooth manifolds and smooth maps
dg.smooth.define: A smooth structure is a maximal atlas whose coordinate changes are smooth. A map between smooth manifolds is smooth when its coordinate representations are smooth.
dg.smooth.statement: A smooth structure is a maximal atlas whose coordinate changes are smooth. A map between smooth manifolds is smooth when its coordinate representations are smooth.
dg.smooth.hypotheses: Manifolds are finite dimensional, Hausdorff and second countable; boundary is excluded unless stated.
dg.smooth.example: The sphere has compatible charts obtained by stereographic projection.
dg.smooth.caution: A homeomorphism need not be a diffeomorphism; topology alone does not specify a smooth structure.
dg.smooth.references:
DG: smooth manifolds and maps.

- **DG** — John M. Lee. [Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~lee/Books/ISM/). Second edition, Springer, 2013; author's page.

dg.tangent.title: Tangent spaces and differentials
dg.tangent.define: Tangent vectors are derivations, and smooth maps differentiate by the chain rule.
dg.tangent.statement: A tangent vector at p is a derivation on germs of smooth functions at p. A smooth map f induces $df_p:T_pM\to T_{f(p)}N$ with $d(g\circ f)_p=dg_{f(p)}\circ df_p$.
dg.tangent.hypotheses: Derivations are linear and satisfy the Leibniz rule.
dg.tangent.example: A curve through p gives a tangent vector by differentiating functions along it.
dg.tangent.caution: A tangent vector is intrinsic; a chosen coordinate tuple is its representation.
dg.tangent.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Smooth manifolds and smooth maps](./notes/dg.smooth.md)
dg.tangent.references:
DG: tangent vectors.

- **DG** — John M. Lee. [Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~lee/Books/ISM/). Second edition, Springer, 2013; author's page.

dg.rank.title: Inverse, implicit and constant-rank theorems
dg.rank.define: An invertible differential gives local smooth coordinates in which a map is a diffeomorphism. A constant-rank map has local normal form consisting of a projection followed by an inclusion.
dg.rank.statement: An invertible differential gives local smooth coordinates in which a map is a diffeomorphism. A constant-rank map has local normal form consisting of a projection followed by an inclusion.
dg.rank.hypotheses: Invertibility is required at the point for the inverse theorem; rank is constant on a neighborhood for the constant-rank theorem.
dg.rank.example: A regular level set of a smooth real-valued function is a codimension-one submanifold.
dg.rank.caution: A critical level can be singular even when the map is smooth.
dg.rank.proof_idea: Apply the Euclidean inverse function theorem to selected coordinate components and solve for the remaining ones.
dg.rank.references:
DG: submersions, immersions and embeddings.

- **DG** — John M. Lee. [Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~lee/Books/ISM/). Second edition, Springer, 2013; author's page.

dg.cotangent.title: Cotangent bundles and tensor fields
dg.cotangent.define: Covectors and tensors encode multilinear data intrinsically on a manifold.
dg.cotangent.statement: The cotangent space is $T_p^*M=\operatorname{Hom}(T_pM,\mathbb R)$. Tensor fields are smooth sections of tensor products of tangent and cotangent bundles.
dg.cotangent.hypotheses: Covariant and contravariant indices transform differently under coordinate changes.
dg.cotangent.example: The differential of a smooth function is a covector field.
dg.cotangent.caution: A metric identifies vectors and covectors only after that metric is chosen.
dg.cotangent.references:
DG: cotangent bundles and tensors.

- **DG** — John M. Lee. [Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~lee/Books/ISM/). Second edition, Springer, 2013; author's page.

dg.flows.title: Vector fields, Lie brackets and flows
dg.flows.define: Vector fields generate local flows; their commutators define the Lie bracket.
dg.flows.statement: A vector field acts as a derivation on smooth functions. Its Lie bracket is $[X,Y]f=X(Yf)-Y(Xf)$. Local flows solve the associated ordinary differential equation.
dg.flows.hypotheses: Local existence and uniqueness use smoothness; global flows require completeness of the vector field.
dg.flows.example: Every smooth vector field on a compact manifold without boundary is complete.
dg.flows.caution: A vector field on a noncompact manifold may escape in finite time.
dg.flows.references:
DG: vector fields and flows.

- **DG** — John M. Lee. [Introduction to Smooth Manifolds](https://sites.math.washington.edu/~lee/Books/ISM/). Second edition, Springer, 2013; author's page.

dg.forms.title: Differential forms and exterior derivative
dg.forms.define: Alternating tensor fields carry a coordinate-independent exterior derivative.
dg.forms.statement: A k-form is a smooth alternating covariant k-tensor. The exterior derivative satisfies $d^2=0$ and $d(\alpha\wedge\beta)=d\alpha\wedge\beta+(-1)^k\alpha\wedge d\beta$.
dg.forms.hypotheses: Here alpha has degree k; pullback commutes with exterior derivative.
dg.forms.example: On the punctured plane, $(-y\,dx+x\,dy)/(x^2+y^2)$ is closed but not exact.
dg.forms.caution: Closed forms need not be globally exact.

**Within this subject**

dg.orientation.title: Orientation and integration
dg.orientation.define: An orientation consistently chooses positive ordered tangent bases. Compactly supported top-degree forms can be integrated on oriented manifolds using oriented charts and a partition of unity.
dg.orientation.statement: An orientation consistently chooses positive ordered tangent bases. Compactly supported top-degree forms can be integrated on oriented manifolds using oriented charts and a partition of unity.
dg.orientation.hypotheses: Integration of forms requires orientation; densities provide a different orientation-free construction.
dg.orientation.example: A nowhere-vanishing top form determines an orientation.
dg.orientation.caution: The Mobius strip admits no global orientation.
dg.orientation.prerequisites:
**Within this subject**

- [Differential forms and exterior derivative](./notes/dg.forms.md)

dg.stokes.title: Stokes' theorem
dg.stokes.define: Integrating an exterior derivative equals integrating the form over the oriented boundary.
dg.stokes.statement: For an oriented smooth n-manifold M with boundary and a compactly supported smooth (n-1)-form omega, $\int_M d\omega=\int_{\partial M}\omega$.
dg.stokes.hypotheses: The boundary orientation uses the outward-normal-first convention; compact support controls behavior at infinity.
dg.stokes.example: The fundamental theorem of calculus and the classical divergence theorem are instances.
dg.stokes.caution: Changing the boundary orientation changes the sign.
dg.stokes.proof_idea: Prove the formula in half-space coordinates and combine the local identities with a partition of unity.
dg.stokes.references:
DG: Stokes theorem.

dg.derham.title: de Rham theorem
dg.derham.define: Differential forms compute real singular cohomology by integration.
dg.derham.statement: Integration of closed forms over smooth singular cycles induces $H^k_{\mathrm{dR}}(M)\cong H^k(M;\mathbb R)$.
dg.derham.hypotheses: M is a smooth manifold; the comparison is with real singular cohomology.
dg.derham.example: A closed one-form on a circle has a nontrivial class when its period is nonzero.
dg.derham.caution: Real differential forms do not detect integral torsion classes.
dg.derham.proof_idea: Use the local Poincare lemma and a Mayer–Vietoris or sheaf argument to pass from local to global.

dg.metric.title: Riemannian metrics
dg.metric.define: A Riemannian metric is a smooth positive-definite inner product on each tangent space. It defines lengths, angles, curve lengths and an induced distance on each connected component.
dg.metric.statement: A Riemannian metric is a smooth positive-definite inner product on each tangent space. It defines lengths, angles, curve lengths and an induced distance on each connected component.
dg.metric.hypotheses: Positive definiteness distinguishes this setting from pseudo-Riemannian geometry.
dg.metric.example: The sphere inherits its round metric from Euclidean space.
dg.metric.caution: Different metrics on the same smooth manifold can have different curvature and completeness.
dg.metric.prerequisites:

dg.levi-civita.title: Levi-Civita connection
dg.levi-civita.define: A Riemannian metric determines a unique torsion-free metric connection.
dg.levi-civita.statement:
Every Riemannian metric has a unique connection with $
abla g=0$ and zero torsion: $
abla_XY-

dg.geodesics.title: Geodesics and the exponential map
dg.geodesics.define: Geodesics have parallel velocity and define the local exponential map.
dg.geodesics.statement: A geodesic satisfies $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$. The exponential map sends an initial vector v to the value at time one of its geodesic, when defined.
dg.geodesics.hypotheses: Local existence and uniqueness follow from the smooth geodesic ODE.
dg.geodesics.example: Great circles are geodesics of the round sphere.
dg.geodesics.caution: Geodesics minimize distance locally, but may cease to minimize globally past a cut point.

dg.curvature.title: Curvature and sectional curvature
dg.curvature.define: Curvature measures the failure of covariant derivatives to commute.
dg.curvature.statement:
Use $R(X,Y)Z=

dg.jacobi.title: Jacobi fields
dg.jacobi.define: Jacobi fields describe first-order separation of nearby geodesics.
dg.jacobi.statement: A variation through geodesics has variation field J satisfying $\nabla_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$. Conversely local Jacobi fields arise from suitable geodesic variations.
dg.jacobi.hypotheses: The curvature convention is the one specified in the curvature entry; derivatives are covariant.
dg.jacobi.example: On the round sphere initially diverging meridians reconverge at the antipode.
dg.jacobi.caution: A conjugate point and a cut point are related but not identical notions.

dg.hopf-rinow.title: Hopf–Rinow theorem
dg.hopf-rinow.define: For a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, metric completeness is equivalent to geodesic completeness and to compactness of closed bounded subsets. Completeness also ensures a minimizing geodesic between any two points.
dg.hopf-rinow.statement: For a connected finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold without boundary, metric completeness is equivalent to geodesic completeness and to compactness of closed bounded subsets. Completeness also ensures a minimizing geodesic between any two points.
dg.hopf-rinow.hypotheses: The metric is the Riemannian length metric; finite dimension is essential.
dg.hopf-rinow.example: A compact Riemannian manifold without boundary is complete.
dg.hopf-rinow.caution: General infinite-dimensional Hilbert manifolds do not satisfy this entire equivalence.

dg.gauss-bonnet.title: Gauss–Bonnet for closed surfaces
dg.gauss-bonnet.define: Total Gaussian curvature of a closed oriented surface is determined by its Euler characteristic.
dg.gauss-bonnet.statement: For a closed oriented Riemannian surface M, $\int_M K\,dA=2\pi\chi(M)$.
dg.gauss-bonnet.hypotheses: K is Gaussian curvature; surfaces with boundary require geodesic-curvature and corner terms.
dg.gauss-bonnet.example: The unit sphere has total curvature 4 pi and Euler characteristic two.
dg.gauss-bonnet.caution: Pointwise curvature depends on the metric even though this total is topological.
dg.gauss-bonnet.proof_idea: Integrate the local curvature identity on a triangulation and sum angle defects; internal boundary terms cancel.

dg.lie.define: A Lie group is a smooth manifold with smooth multiplication and inverse. Left-invariant vector fields identify its tangent space at the identity with a Lie algebra.

dg.bundles.title: Vector bundles and connections

dg.bundles.statement: A vector bundle is locally a product with a fixed vector space and linear transition maps. A connection differentiates sections with $\nabla(fs)=df\otimes s+f\nabla s$.

dg.sard.title: Sard's theorem and regular values
dg.sard.define: For a smooth map between finite-dimensional smooth manifolds, the set of critical values has measure zero in every target coordinate chart.
dg.sard.statement: For a smooth map between finite-dimensional smooth manifolds, the set of critical values has measure zero in every target coordinate chart.

dg.hodge.title: Hodge theorem
dg.hodge.define: On a closed oriented Riemannian manifold, cohomology classes have unique harmonic representatives.
dg.hodge.statement: On a closed oriented Riemannian manifold, each real de Rham cohomology class has exactly one harmonic representative, annihilated by $\Delta=dd^*+d^*d$.
dg.hodge.hypotheses: Compactness without boundary and the Riemannian metric are part of this statement.
dg.hodge.example: The dimension of harmonic k-forms equals the kth real Betti number.

ag.rings.define: All rings here are commutative with identity and maps preserve identity. An ideal absorbs multiplication by ring elements; a module is the corresponding linear structure with scalars in a ring.

ag.noetherian.title: Noetherian rings and Hilbert basis theorem
ag.noetherian.define: A ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated. If A is Noetherian, its polynomial ring in finitely many variables is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.statement: A ring is Noetherian exactly when every ideal is finitely generated. If A is Noetherian, its polynomial ring in finitely many variables is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.hypotheses: The equivalence uses the ascending chain condition on ideals.
ag.noetherian.example: Every finitely generated algebra over a field is Noetherian.
ag.noetherian.caution: A polynomial ring in infinitely many variables over a field is not Noetherian.

ag.localization.title: Localization and local rings
ag.localization.define: Localization inverts selected ring elements and focuses algebra near a prime ideal.
ag.localization.statement: For a multiplicative subset S, $S^{-1}A$ universally makes elements of S invertible. Localizing at $S=A\setminus\mathfrak p$ gives the local ring $A_{\mathfrak p}$ with maximal ideal $\mathfrak p A_{\mathfrak p}$.
ag.localization.hypotheses: A local ring has a unique maximal ideal; localization may be the zero ring if zero lies in S.
ag.localization.example: $\mathbb Z_{(p)}$ consists of rationals whose denominators are not divisible by p.

ag.nullstellensatz.title: Hilbert Nullstellensatz
ag.nullstellensatz.define: Over an algebraically closed field, polynomial zero sets correspond to radical ideals.
ag.nullstellensatz.statement: Over an algebraically closed field k, maximal ideals of $k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]$ are point ideals and $I(V(I))=\sqrt I$.
ag.nullstellensatz.hypotheses: The field must be algebraically closed; the number of variables is finite.
ag.nullstellensatz.example: Over $\mathbb C$, the ideal $(x^2)$ and its radical $(x)$ have the same zero set.
ag.nullstellensatz.caution: Point sets alone do not retain nilpotent structure.
ag.nullstellensatz.proof_idea: Zariski's lemma proves the maximal-ideal statement; the Rabinowitsch trick deduces the radical statement.

ag.affine.title: Affine varieties and coordinate rings
ag.affine.define: Affine geometry is encoded contravariantly by coordinate rings.
ag.affine.statement: For an affine algebraic set X over an algebraically closed field, $k[X]=k[x_1,\ldots,x_n]/I(X)$. Regular maps correspond contravariantly to k-algebra homomorphisms of coordinate rings.
ag.affine.hypotheses: Here variety means a reduced irreducible finite-type object, so its coordinate ring is a domain; reducible algebraic sets are also allowed when named as such.

ag.riemann-roch.title: Riemann–Roch for curves
ag.riemann-roch.define: Riemann–Roch balances sections, divisor degree and genus on smooth projective curves.
ag.riemann-roch.statement: For a divisor D on a smooth projective geometrically integral curve of genus g over an algebraically closed field, $\ell(D)-\ell(K_C-D)=\deg D+1-g$, where $\ell(D)=\dim H^0(C,\mathcal O_C(D))$.
ag.riemann-roch.hypotheses: K_C is a canonical divisor; degree and genus use the curve's smooth projective structure.
ag.riemann-roch.caution: The same formula without correction does not apply to arbitrary singular or nonproper curves.
ag.riemann-roch.proof_idea: Compute the Euler characteristic by adding points to a divisor and use Serre duality to identify the H1 term.

ag.serre-duality.title: Serre duality on curves
ag.serre-duality.define: The canonical bundle pairs first cohomology with a dual space of sections.
ag.serre-duality.statement: For a line bundle L on a smooth projective geometrically integral curve C over k, $H^1(C,L)$ is naturally dual to $H^0(C,\omega_C\otimes L^{-1})$.
ag.serre-duality.hypotheses: Finite-dimensionality and the dualizing canonical bundle use properness and smoothness in this version.
ag.serre-duality.example: Applying this to the structure sheaf identifies the genus with the dimension of regular differentials.
ag.serre-duality.caution: For singular schemes one needs a dualizing object rather than blindly substituting the sheaf of differentials.
ag.serre-duality.proof_idea: The trace map on H1 of the canonical bundle turns cup product into a perfect pairing.
